Heading: Villagers vandalise liquor vend - Indian Express
Content:
A day after World Tourism Day was celebrated in the city amid much fanfare, a 20-year-old German tourist was allegedly kidnapped and molested by six youth.

According to the police, the youths, in a black Mahindra Scorpio (HR 582123), kidnapped the German national from the parking lot of the Hotel Taj GVK, Sector 17, around 2 am on Sunday.

The girl had come out of the hotel to smoke and was reportedly in an inebriated state.

"According to the Taj's security guards, one of the youth had a brief conversation with the girl. They pulled her into the Scorpio and sped away," said a police officer.

Around 3 pm on Sunday, two of the accused dropped her at one of her friend's house in Sector 20 in a white Maruti 800 (HR 01-S-8874).

A case on charges of kidnapping and molestation has been registered against the accused at Sector-17 police station. The Chandigarh Police have rounded up a few suspects, who were subjected to interrogation.

A senior police officer said they were trying to trace both the vehicles used in the incident on the basis of their registration numbers.

"Raids are being conducted at various places in Punjab and Haryana to nab the accused. The perpetrators have been identified and will be arrested soon," the police officer added.

"The girl sustained several injuries after the accused tried to rape her in the night. A medical examination of the victim will be conducted to ascertain whether she was raped. The matter is under investigation," said Assistant Superintendent of Police, Madhur Verma.

The victim had come to Chandigarh on September 23 with her friends Hardeep Singh and Ina. Hardeep and Ina, a German national, got married last week and a reception party was scheduled for Sunday night.

According to the police, the trio had gone to Hotel Taj late on Saturday night for coffee and drinks.

When the victim did not return, Hardeep informed the Police Control Room. Messages were flashed all over, but the police failed to intercept the Mahindra Scorpio.

The girl's statement

The victim told the police that she had gone out of the hotel for a puff, when she was approached by a youngster. He pushed her into the rear seat of the vehicle, where one of the accused sat over her and three others pushed her face into the seat so that she could not scream. They kept driving for about 90 minutes to two hours, after which she was taken to a house in the fields. She was shifted to another room from there and stripped. Then the accused tried to rape her. When the girl resisted, she was mercilessly beaten. According to the girl, the accused did not rape her. Around 9 am on Sunday, they started from the unidentified location and drove around for about three-four hours. Then, she was transported to a white Maruti and dropped in Sector 20." The police are facing a tough time questioning the victim as she does not know much English.

Heading: ‘Delivery of justice has been reduced to a business’ - Indian Express
Content:
On September 25, Surinder Singh was allegedly beaten up by the vend employees. Singh died on Sunday

Angry residents reportedly vandalised a liquor vend in Darua village after its employees allegedly beat a man to death.

Around 3.30 pm today, a mob of around 50 people smashed liquor bottles, looted the store and bashed up the staff.

The injured employees — Ajay, Darbara, Karan and Ashok — were admitted to Government Medical College and Hospital, Sector 32.

A case of rioting, hurt and criminal trespass was registered against unidentified persons for vandalising the vend.

The commotion started when 36-year-old Surinder Singh succumbed to his injuries at the PGI today. Singh was admitted to the hospital in a critical condition on Saturday. At that time, the deceased's family had told the doctors that he was injured in an accident.

During treatment, Surinder said he was mercilessly beaten by the staff at the liquor vend on September 25. He was accompanied by Devi Singh, an employee with the UT electricity board.

Surinder claimed that the staff had refused him a bottle of beer stating the vend had closed for the night.

A scuffle ensued wherein the employees thrashed Surinder while Devi Singh managed to flee.

A case under Section 304 (culpable homicide not amounting to murder) has been registered on a complaint lodged by the deceased's brother, Narinder Singh.

Station House Officer, Industrial Area Police Station,Yashpal Sharma said: "With Devi Singh's help, we hope to identify the accused soon."

Heading: ‘We are just separated by borders’ - Indian Express
Content:
Taking strong note of the deteriorating state of the country's judicial system, Supreme Court judge Justice G S Singhvi, today said justice delivery has now been reduced to a mere business in the eyes of the people. Recalling the days of freedom struggle, Sanghvi said there was a time when lawyers fought not for money, but for sacrifice. "Be it lawyers or judges, have we forgotten our task towards society?" he asked.

Adding that judges these days are bent more towards counting the number of cases they have disposed of, instead of impartial delivery of justice, Justice Sanghvi emphasised the need to redefine the role of judges in society.

Addressing a seminar on 'The responsibility of judicial system towards society' organised by the Intellectual Associations Chandigarh, Justice Sanghvi said that due to the harassment a common man suffers in his pursuit of justice, 95 per cent of the masses avoid going to courts at all and choose to suffer silently. "The five per cent who do go wait in queue for many long years and empty out their pockets to hire a lawyer. It is a nightmare for the common man to approach a higher court," he said, adding that this is the reason people have started taking the law in their hands.

Throwing light on the common problem of delayed justice, he rued that the enormous delay in trials has shattered the public's confidence in the judiciary.

He also recalled an incident where a lady wrote to him that she was granted bail, but as she was unable to furnish a sum of Rs 2,000 as security, she spent another year in jail. "Have we become totally insensitive? Each one of us needs to join hands to contribute towards justice," he said.

"We have the best brains in the world, the best of doctors, but the largest number of HIV-infected patients. Despite a large number of millionaires, yet the maximum of poor — we have the best and yet some of the worst."

Justice Singhvi urged people to initiate a second freedom movement to save the nation. "We have lost sight of the great teachers who were the builders of our society. We forgot the engineers who built modern India. The time has come to stop glorifying ourselves and talk about our duty towards society," he added.

Heading: Senior citizens walk to keep their hearts healthy - Indian Express
Content:
"India is not just any other country, but a heaven on earth," says Nadeh Ali, a member of the students' delegation from Pakistan that is in Chandigarh to participate in the International Students' Peace Festival.

The students from Pakistan stepped on the Indian soil on Saturday with mixed emotions. "But the warmth that we have received from the people here has washed away all our apprehensions. The hospitality being extended to us is overwhelming," says Shayan Shaikh, a student from Lahore. Ask about the city and the one hears a chorus — 'splendid'.

"The city is similar to Islamabad with all the greenery and roundabouts," says Risham Ahmad while adding that Sikh boys are "very attractive" and "wearing the pag adds to their charm".

Girls on two-wheelers are, however, a 'rare sight' for them. "Back home, we do not even ride cycles, only cars. It was amusing to see girls driving scooters," says another student Zikra Baloch.

Drawing a relation between the cultures of the two countries, Shabbir, a student-cum-social activist says, "Though the traditions are almost similar, here it is more vibrant and rich. Indian food is very delicious, though it seems that there is more vegetarianism here. The spices and herbs make the food here very tempting."

Bollywood superstar Shahrukh Khan enjoys mass popularity in Pakistan as well. "I am a huge fan of Shah Rukh and do not miss any of his movies. We regularly watch Hindi movies for all the song and dance routine and the glamour is captivating," says a student Shayan.

For these students, the hostility between the two countries is politically manifested. "My purpose to visit India is to tell people that Muslims are not terrorists. Because of a handful of fanatics, the entire community has been maligned. The media is projecting us in a very demeaning way which is very hurting," says a student Nadeh.

He adds "We want Indians to visit us and overcome their apprehensions as we are essentially the same, just separated by borders."

Students' peace festival kicks off

The third International Students' Peace Festival kicked off on Sunday with a cultural programme at DAV College, Sector 10. Union minister of state for finance and parliamentary affairs, Pawan Kumar Bansal, was the chief guest on the occasion. Nearly 200 students from various countries, including Pakistan and Nepal, will participate in the festival that aims at providing a platform to young minds for exchage of ideas. Addressing the audience on the importance of harmony among the countries, Bansal said, "We need to move on with time and forget the animosity between the two countries, India and Pakistan. Peace festivals like these offer first hand opportunity to the young to know each other, and make bridges where efforts of the elders have failed." H S Mattewal, Advocate General (Punjab), harped on global threats of terror and the relevance of maintaining peace during the critical period. The cultural programme organised on the occasion had various items including Tamil dance and Punjabi Bolis presented by students of DAV School, Amritsar. While on a sightseeing tour of the city, the guests also visited the Rock Garden and Sukhna Lake. Abbas Ali from South Asia Partnership, Pakistan, Mubashir Mirza, Chairman CYDA, Mayor Pardeep Chhabra and Ram Chander from Nepal also addressed the students.

Heading: At Badal’s sangat darshan, general public kept at bay - Indian Express
Content:
With an aim to create awareness among senior citizens about various health problems, World Heart Day was celebrated at the Day Care Centre, Senior Citizens Council, Panchkula, on Sunday. The participants at the event discussed their health problems with a team of experts.

"World Heart Day was celebrated in the council for the first time. The main idea behind such an initiative is to spread awareness among senior citizens to keep them healthy and fit," said Lt Col B M Talwar, president, Senior Citizen Council, Panchkula.

The event was inaugurated by Deputy Commissioner (Panchklula) Rajinder Kataria who marked the day by planting a sapling on the council premises. It was followed by a 'healthy heart walk' by the members under the leadership of Lt Col Talwar from the Senior Citizen Council office to the Community Centre, Sector 15, Panchkula.

"The problem of stress needs to be addressed at the initial stages before it worsens. It is the cause of many other problems pertaining to the heart and mind. Many researches on stress are being undertaken in different Indian medical institutes that will benefit the public at large," said Dr Aditya Rattan, consultant cardiologist, Heart Line.

The other doctors in the panel of speakers were Dr Vijay Girdhar, a psychiatrist and Dr Sandeep Jassal of Live Life More foundation.

The event ended with a special prize announced for the oldest healthy heart that was given to an 84-year-old senior citizen.

Heading: Vodafone executive’s murder: Cops work on ‘vital clues’ - Indian Express
Content:
The Patiala District Administration played a spoilsport at the sangat darshan programme held by Chief Minister Parkash Singh Badal. They made it sure that sangat and mediapersons stay away from the venue. Badal was in the city for the fourth phase of issuing grants and said his government will spend Rs 550 crore to give better facilities to villages.

Following orders of Patiala Deputy Commissioner Vikas Garg and other senior police officials, security persons created numerous hindrances for the public who had come all the way to meet the chief minister.

"Show us the card signed by the Patiala SSP and DC, only then you can meet the chief minister," said a constable to one of the invited mediapersons.

Even after being invited by the District Public Relations Office to cover the function, the security men not only misbehaved but refused to allow journalists and camerapersons inside the venue. Later, Badal's media advisor HS Bains assured mediapersons to look into the matter.

The chief minister said Dalits were mistreated by the Congress during their regime, who did not bother to extend any facilities to the community. "We have made Charanjit Attwal the deputy speaker, who is from this community," he said.

Asked if the state was on high alert, Badal said the cops were always vigilant. "The intelligence wing does not have a thermometer to nab the real culprits all the time but are doing their best," said Badal.

Heading: This chef loves to dish out innovative menus - Indian Express
Content:
The Mohali police on Sunday claimed to have got vital clues and working on different theories to crack the brutal murder of a customer care executive of Intelnet, a call centre of leading mobile service provider Vodafone, in Phase V on Saturday night.

Devinder Kumar Sahota, 24, of Shivalik Avenue Ataya Nangal in Ropar was stabbed by three unidentified men after he resisted the bid to snatch his mobile phone.

Preliminary investigations have ruled out any love triangle, service dispute, personal enmity or bad character behind the gruesome killing, Phase I Station House Officer (SHO) Harbir Singh, who is the investigating officer (IO), told Newsline.

The SHO said that the autopsy examination conducted at the Civil Hospital on Sunday revealed that Devinder died due to heart puncture. One of the three miscreants had stabbed Devinder numerous times on his head, chest, left forearm and wrist, said the IO.

Devinder and his colleague Sandeep Dogra, also in his mid-20s, were intercepted by three motorcycle-borne youths near the bus stop in Phase V at 9.30 pm. Taking Devinder's mobile phone on the pretext of making a call, the assilants fled away, the SHO said.

As the miscreants tried to speed away with Devinder's mobile phone, he caught hold of one of them. The unidentified man then stabbed Devinder with a dagger, said the SHO. Devinder was declared dead on arrival at the Civil Hospital by the Emergency Medical Officer Dr Harmeet.

Sources revealed that the assailants left the dagger used in the crime. A case has been lodged against three unidentified youth at Phase-I police station.

Heading: Man alleges abduction by armymen, SHO says case ‘very petty’ - Indian Express
Content:
The minute the alarm beeps at 6.15 am, Neeraj Chaudhry, is up and about. This executive chef at the Taj Hotel, who stays in Sector 38, admits to never having missed his exercise schedule. "Owing to the beautiful parks near my house, the three-kilometre walk becomes all the more enjoyable," says Neeraj, who is back home by 7 am, just in time to wake his daughter.

"I make sure that I spend time with my six-year-old daughter in the morning," he says. An hour later, its time to head for work. "I reach the hotel between 8.15 and 8.30 am, and then make way through the various sections, greeting staff and taking part in conversation with them," says the chef.

Having made a round of the kitchen, its time for the daily meeting. It's here that the day's schedule is discussed. "We are appraised about the important guests for the day, the functions and our scores on the guest satisfaction tracking system," he says.

Meeting over, its time to head back to the kitchen once again. "This is one of the most hectic time. Lunch is being prepared for the buffet along with banquet menus. I move from one department to another, overlooking the work and even pitching in if required," says Chaudhry, who is on his feet till 1 pm. That over, he settles in the staff cafeteria for lunch. After 1.30 pm, he steps into his office gets busy answering his mails, before shooting off to the hotel's restaurants, checking on the menu, the guests and the kitchen, all at one go.

"After lunch has been dealt with, I move to the banquet and meet the manager. Banquets bring in huge revenues and are one of the most important sources of revenue," says the chef.

Back to his office by 5 pm, he spends an hour, sitting back and deciding on the menu. "This is the one hour in the day that I look forward to as I get to sit back and think of new dishes, plan innovative menus and get creative," he remarks. In between, he files his daily report before shutting the computer at 7. With dinner time nearing, he once again visits the kitchen, takes a stock of the bookings, expected guests and checks if all is in place. "I call it a day at 9.30 pm and head home, where I have the day's first cup of tea with my wife," says Neeraj.

At home, he dines with his wife while preparing for the next day, which he calls "making notes".

Heading: Land and infrastructure granted, Panchkula Technology Park awaits construction - Indian Express
Content:
High drama was witnessed at the Airport Chowk on Sunday when a resident of Sector 15, Sanjeev Nehra, was allegedly 'abducted' by the occupants of an army truck ands harassed by them at a transit camp for nearly an hour following a road accident. The victim's wife, Shruti Nehra, along with their three-year-old son, meanwhile, looked around for her husband who disappeared in no time.

The couple was on its way to Patiala when their car (CH03M 7033) collided with an army truck at the Airport Chowk. When Sanjeev confronted the driver of the truck for hitting their car, some army persons allegedly started misbehaving with the couple. When Shruti came back to the car to call the police, she was shocked to see the truck and her husband missing from the spot.

"They forced him in their car and took him away to their transit camp. A time came when his phone was also switched off and there was no contact with him. He returned on foot after an hour," said Shruti.

When the victim returned and approached the police to lodge a complaint, no case was registered. Instead, the police allegedly tried their best to settle a compromise even as the victim cried foul against the manhandling by the army persons.

When contacted, Station House Officer (SHO), Sector 31 police station, Bhupinder Singh, said a compromise has been reached and dismissed the incident as a "very petty" case. "It was nothing. We have received no complaint," added the SHO.

Shruti, meanwhile, demanded police action against the harassment faced by them for which, they will also deposit a complaint at the public window.

Heading: Phalgu Tirath to be developed for tourism - Indian Express
Content:
Despite the entire infrastructure having been provided by the Haryana State Industrial Development Corporation (HSIIDC) and four months since it allotted plots to various IT companies, none have started construction at the Panchkula Technology Park (PTP).

This is, however, not great news for the HSIIDC authorities, both for the existing phase and the second phase of the park, for which it got 162.4 acres of land approved from the Haryana Urban Development Authority (HUDA).

Of the 23 companies allotted plots in the IT Park, none have initiated any development work till now. The total area under possession in the park in Phase I, being spread over an area of 74.62 acres, is divided into 23 plots of various sizes into two categories. A ten-acre plot under the campus development scheme has been allotted to a real estate developing company while 22 plots of different sizes under the self user category have been allotted to the 'so called' IT companies.

"Infrastructure facilities like roads, sewerage, water supply, drainage and streetlights has been provided by the HSIIDC, which is now waiting for the companies to start construction. The offer of possession was granted from June after the allotments were given to the companies but no company has started construction or even expressed interest to initiate the same, till date ," said the official spokesperson of HSIIDC.

An official of one of the 23 companies said that possession has been given to 21 companies, which had been allotted plots in the PTP. These companies unlike the Chandigarh Technology Park are not 'bigwigs'.

The companies allotted plots justify the delay in construction by stating the lapse on part of the HSIIDC. "We had been waiting for the construction norms from the HSIIDC, which we have not received till date. We will start the work as soon as we receive it as we are not aware of the built-up to open area ratio specifications," said one of the senior officials of Altruist Technologies Pvt. Ltd., one of the companies allotted plot Number 2 at the Panchkula Technology Park.

Heading: Illegal mining in Aravalis continues despite ban - Indian Express
Content:
Haryana Chief Minister Bhupinder Singh Hooda today announced to constitute a Phalgu Tirath Board to develop Phalgu Tirath in Pharal village in view of its religious importance. An amount on Rs 50 lakh would be spent on the development works of Phalgu Tirath, situated in village Pharal.

After taking a dip in the holy sarovar of Phalgu Tirath ghat, Hooda said the state government had taken many initiatives to renovate temples and develop all religious places in the state and a huge amount had been spent on the renovation of temples at Kurukshetra, Pehowa and Kalayat. "Now the famous Phalgu Tirath would be developed on the same pattern," he said.

Hooda also performed pind-daan and offered prayers on the occasion. Kalyat MLA Geeta Bhukal, DC Vikas Gupta, SP Sultan Singh and other officers were also present on this occasion.

The district administration has made elaborate arrangements to facilitate the large number of pilgrims who would be visiting the Phalgu Tirth for a holy dip. Above 10 lakh pilgrims have already taken a holy dip in the sarovar so far and it was expected that about five lakh pilgrims would take a holy dip on the occasionof somvati amavas on the concluding day of the mela.

Heading: Farmers threaten to step up stir - Indian Express
Content:
Despite several measures undertaken by the state government in the past to check illegal mining in Aravalis, the menace has continued to haunt the state. Taking a serious view of the on going illegal mining, the state government has now directed the regional officers of the Haryana Pollution Control Board (HPCB) to constitute a committee for a strict vigil on any illegal activity in the Aravali range.

The regional officers of the HPCB have been asked to submit a videographed report by the end of next month to provide documentary proof of all such wrong doings in the Aravalis which are a threat to the environment.

Minister of State for Tourism, Environment and Forests, Kiran Choudhary, who presided over a meeting of the state pollution control board, asked the officers to take strict action against those involved in such activities. The officers have been asked to submit a regular report on such activities to keep the department well-informed.

The Supreme Court, in its order, had banned mining in the areas around Delhi and the Aravalis because of pollution and threat to ecological balance caused by it. However, mining activities have increased in the recent years. With the 2010 Commonwealth Games scheduled to be held in Delhi, construction activities has increased in Delhi and surrounding areas. The usage of stones and other materials has increased as a result.

UPA Chairperson Sonia Gandhi, in a letter to the Haryana government, asked for stopping of illegal mining activities Aravalis. But the Bhupinder Singh Hooda government failed to keep a check on the illegal mining activities, according to sources.

Talking to The Indian Express, Kiran Choudhary said the Bhupinder Singh Hooda government is very serious about checking illegal mining in the state. "Illegal mining is a threat to ecology. It is an offence against mother nature. We are trying our best to put a stop to illegal mining. The photographic evidence would be crucial in prosecution of the offenders in the future,'' she said.

Choudhary has asked the officers concerned to take strict action against those violating the law. The regional officers should take up cases of violations and prosecutions against such persons should be launched at the earliest, she said.

According to sources, it is not easy to put a check on illegal mining in the Aravalis as the violaters are protected by some powerful leaders in the state. "No one is above law. Anybody who defies law would have to face the consequences,'' the minister said.

Heading: A treat awaits the tourists: CM - Indian Express
Content:
Pledging to continue their agitation against the government's decision to implement the master plan in Baddi-Barotiwala-Nalagarh industrial belt, hundreds of farmers and elected representatives of panchayti raj institutions held a maha-panchayat to register their protest at Nalagarh, on Saturday.

The maha panchayat today unanimously passed a resolution urging the government to withdraw its decision in the larger interests of farming community.

Notably, the government had invited objections from the villagers by September 30 before implementing the master plan in Buddi-Barotiwala-Nalagarh industrial area.The proposal to implement the master plan was moved by the previous Congress government in order to provide basic amenities, strengthen infrastructure and ensure planned growth of the area, two years ago.

After this, the master plan was prepared by the officials of concerned department. Under the plan, the government had proposed a total width of internal roads from five to 15 metres, 24 metres of main roads, 45 metres of state highways and 60 meters of the national highway.

The master plan would be implemented in 229 villages including Nagar Parishad, Baddi, and Municipal Committee, Nalagarh, over 318 sq km area.

The farmers at the maha panchayat also demanded compensation to the farmers as per the prevailing market prices of the land, being acquired for the purpose of setting up of industries and widening of roads in the area.

The meeting also demanded scrapping of change of land use, translation of master plan in Hindi language and relaxation of norms in Town and Country Planning Act.

Heading: Himachal confidential - Indian Express
Content:
Himachal is ready to give the tourists an experience different from the conventional tourism by involving sectors such a rural tourism, heritage, adventure, horticulture and eco-tourism, said Chief Minister Prem Kumar Dhumal while presiding over the valedictory function of the World Tourism Week celebrations held here.

"Himachal is making efforts to cater to need of the hour and in the process the state has started Home Stay-2008 scheme that would provide employment to the rural youth and opportunity to tourists to have direct experience of rural life and culture", said Dhumal. He later launched updated website of Himachal tourism that has been developed by Voice of Himachal. The freshly updated websites is redone with focus on tourists' needs.

Heading: Devotees of Rhythm divine - Indian Express
Content:
Wanted: a chief guest

It is a season of annual functions in educational institutions. Many prestigious schools in Shimla are facing the problem of having a high profile chief guest for the functions, of whom there seems to be a shortage. When recently a school invited Chief Minister, another in a bid to outdo the former invited the Governor. But the latter is now reported to be giving its decision a re-think in view of the logistic hassles like comfortable furniture, security and easy access to the venue for the chief guest, which is all being checked by the officials of the Governor House.

A balancing act

The film crews arriving in the town is a sure sign that life in Shimla is limping back to normalcy after it had been thrown out of gear by heavy rains recently. But the situation has put a senior officer in Shimla Municipal Corporation is in a fix. While on one hand, he strives hard to put the civic amenities back on track to alleviate the hardships of the residents, on the other he struggles to keep the bureaucrats in good humour by fixing meetings of their families with film stars like Kareena Kapoor and Saif Ali Khan.

Party mania

The Government Dental College in Shimla recently went overboard in treating some external examiners that they called back some of the examiners who had left for their homes after finishing their duties. One of the examiners who returned from almost near Chandigarh was given a gift pack of HPMC products. But the box slipped from his hand, and all the bottles fell and broke. Embarrassed, the Health Minister, who was also present at the party, promised the examiner of getting the gift replaced.

Getting used to 'no work'

A bureaucrat, who was posted in a frontline public sector undertaking (PSU) by the BJP government soon after it returned to power, is back in the department from where he was transferred. After being removed from the PSU, the officer was not given any posting as a punishment, but now even after taking charge of old office, he is hardy seen in the office. To this one of the staff members commented, "Sahab ko without posting rehne ki adapt toh nahin pad gayi?"

Heading: The real deal - Indian Express
Content:
Earlier thought to be the domain of men with snow-white beard, Gurmat Sangeet has been attracting young boys and girls of Punjab. With Punjabi University, Patiala, starting a professional course in the devotional music genre and demand for qualified raagis increasing abroad, youngsters are getting attached to their roots through music and also eking out a living, finds

With the demand for professional raagis increasing worldwide, hundreds of youths from rural Punjab are carving out a mellifluous career by getting trained in the divine music genre at the Department of Gurmat Sangeet at Punjabi University in Patiala.

The department, which offers a post-graduate course in Gurmat Sangeet, teaches students all the ragas and hymns contained in the Guru Granth Sahib and raga-based kirtan chaukis, as per the maryada. As some of the students take up jobs in overseas gurdwaras, workshops on communication skills in English are also held.

With the department helping students imbibe traditional Sikh values, it has allayed the fear of many Sikh parents, who felt that their children were turning away from their culture. Parents of Saurab Meet Singh, a resident of Patran who is getting trained in taus instrument, feared that their son would wean away from Sikhism and adopt the Western culture after joining college. "I feel attached to Sikhism after I joined the department. I think the Gurus preached in the simplest form. And now, my parents are contented," he said.

Besides the gurdwaras of the country, including the Golden Temple, Sikh missionaries and temples in Europe, Singapore, Canada and the USA recruit professional granthis from Punjab and are ready to give hefty pay packages.

Apart from the divine connection that this genre provides, students get a chance to go abroad riding on this degree. "With this course, getting a visa and work permit in a foreign country becomes easy, besides the job is respectable. This is adding to the popularity of the course. Every year, we get more than 25 students in each group," Dr Gurnam Singh, head of the department, said.

"Employers want that students should be well-versed in English, so that they can train others abroad. Therefore, we have made English compulsory in the syllabus," he added.

"Though it is hard to teach English to these students, most of whom are from the rural background, they understand that once absorbed by gurdwaras abroad, it will be an asset for them," said Amanjot Kaur, an English teacher.

Students, Rajender Kaur, Kamaljit Singh and Pardeep Singh, who are studying for a bachelors degree in Gurmat Sangeet, said no one in their families was in this field, but they wanted to adopt it as a profession. "Rabab, tanpura, sarangi, israj, dilruba and tabla that the Sikh Gurus used to preach had been consigned to oblivion. But the department has revived the traditional art form," they added.

According to a senior ragi, Gurdev Singh, who had earlier served at the Golden Temple, Gurmat Sangeet was pushed into forgetfulness by unqualified teachers and self-styled Sikh kirtankaaris. "Raag parbandh, singing style and prescribed string instruments are very important and only professionals can do justice to it," he said.

As the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee (SGPC) and the Delhi Sikh Gurdwara Management Committee (DSGMC) do not produce professional raagis for their gurdwaras, the department is catering to their huge demand too.

"One of our seniors is earning over $ 3,000 per month as a Gurmat Sangeet teacher in Singapore," said Sunita, a student who hails from Khambra village in Jalandhar. However, she added that though women were not allowed to perform kirtans in gurdwaras, she could secure a job in schools and colleges as a trainer.

Notably, the department, set up in 2004, was the brainchild of Bibi Jasbir Kaur Khalsa, former Vice-Chancellor Swarn Singh Boparai and Gurnam Singh. "While Bibi Khalsa of Guru Gian Parkash Foundation looked after the financial aspects, the V-C helped in setting up the chair and lookied into our problems," said

Dr Gurnam.

"We have 97 per cent placements in various gurdwaras, colleges, schools and music academies across the globe," said Kawaljit Singh, who teaches vocal music.

Unlike Indian classical music, Gurmat Sangeet could not evolve into a distinct discipline due to self-styled teachers and their poor knowledge. Then, Punjabi University stepped in to salvage the lost art. "It is a very difficult tradition, as the prestige and responsibility of the professionals lie in preparing qualified kirtankars, who can help spread the fragrance of Gurbani," said former V-C Swarn Singh Boparai.

Punjabi University Vice-Chancellor Jaspal Singh said the Gurmat Sangeet Department was one of its kind in the world.

The university has also constituted Gurmat Sangeet Development Committee for patronising and guiding the Gurmat Sangeet project. The committee comprises Surinder Singh Bandhu, Bhai Ashok Singh Baagrian, Jasbir Kaur Khalsa, Uttam Singh, Jaspal Singh, Ajit Singh Paintal, Jodh Singh, Jagir Singh and Jaswant Singh.

What's Gurmat Sangeet?

According to Gurnam Singh, Gurmat Sangeet was made popular by the first Guru Nanak Dev, who preached along with his disciple Bhai Mardana, a rababi. "All the Sikh Gurus used poetry and certain musical instruments to sermonise," he added.

Plans

The department plans to launch online teaching of 'G-music' (Gurmat Sangeet) along with short-term certificate courses for NRIs and others. President of Sikh Leher America, a US-based organisation, Harbhajan Singh has started a Rs 1,500-per month scholarship for students.

Achievements

The department is ready with a devotional musical album, featuring topmost names from the Indian music industry. "While Jagjit Singh is composing the music, Sonu Nigam, Roop Kumar Rathod, Hans Raj Hans, Hariharan, Shankar Mahadevan and Ashwani Bhende will lend their voices to it," said Gurnam. Besides, a seven-CD album on Gurmat Sangeet has been completed and it features teachers and students of this department.

Milestone

Due to the initiative of the department, kirtans at the Golden Temple have started including a musician and traditional singers, thus increasing job opportunities. "We had offered a proposal in this regard to SGPC president Avtar Singh Makkar, and he accepted it," said Gurnam.

Instruments

The department had to conduct numerous researches before they could actually find the original instruments that were used by the Gurus. "While Guru Nanak Dev used rabab, Guru Amardas and Guru Arjun Dev took the help of saranda. Guru Hargobind reinvented taus, while Guru Teg Bahadur experimented with mridang and Guru Gobind Singh made dilruba and tanpura important partners in the musical journey," said Ali Akbar, a rabab teacher.

Heading: A decade of searching - Indian Express
Content:
What happens when two people who met with similar fates come together? They relive history. That is what journalists Kuldip Nayar and Asif Noorani did at the launch of their book Tales of Two Cities (Roli) at the India International Centre: they went back to a moment in 1947 when two nations were born in blood, forcing them to leave their land, cross a new, hastily drawn-up border and find homes in unaccustomed earth.

Karachi-based Noorani, associated with the Dawn Group, was in Bombay and all of five when Partition happened. "I vividly recall shouting 'Up, Up the National Flag, Down, Down the Union Jack' as a schoolboy. When someone asked me why I wanted the Union Jack down, in all my innocence, I replied that since Jack fell down and broke his crown, the Union Jack must also come down," laughed Noorani, offering a light moment.

Noorani's family left Bombay for Pakistan only in 1950 when the wounds were not so raw, but Nayar was not so fortunate. He was 24 when he left his hometown of Sialkot, exactly a month after the city became part of Pakistan, and saw first-hand the trauma of migration.

"Circumstances no longer sheltered us in our hometown. Our patience had exhausted in a month, though we came over to Delhi with the idea of returning when things got better. But they only worsened," says Nayar, who started the annual candlelight vigil at Wagah on the night of August 14.

The mood is reflected on the pages where personal stories intertwine with history: if Nayar's "From Sialkot to Delhi" is grim, Noorani's "From Bombay to Karachi' carries twists of humour.

Heading: In tiger’s den - Indian Express
Content:
For 10 years all of us have had a common address—www. google.com

Ten years ago the world's most famous search engine originated as a research project at Stanford University in California. Students Larry Page and Sergey Brin started out by nicknaming it BackRub then. Ten years later, people know it as the thing that changed their lives. It's called Google. Although Brin has famously said, "We are currently not planning to conquer the world," the engine, perhaps, couldn't help doing exactly that. Mapping the way forward, under the slogan 'Don't be evil', the Google guys touch lives without making a big deal about it.

A quick look at the Google products we use, perhaps with the same regularity as we brush our teeth, helps put things in perspective. Within search options there's Alerts, Blog Search, Book Search, Chrome, Desktop Search, Earth, Finance, GOOG-411, Health, iGoogle, Images, Maps, News, Notebook, Patent Search, Product Search,

Scholar, Special Searches, Toolbar, Video, YouTube and Web Search. If you like to explore and innovate choose from the following; Code, Custom Search and Labs. Enabling communication are Blogger, Calendar, Docs, Gmail, Groups, Knol, Orkut, Picasa, Reader, Sites, SketchUp, Talk and Translate. For mobile phones, they have services like Maps for mobile, Mobile Mobile and SMS. Exhaustive, ain't it?

Welcome to Google.com, the most important American invention, since Columbus discovered America itself. Thanks to it, India can take the credit for her Google Musician, Pritam. Lifting sound and rhythms has never been easier. However, for more original people like Luke Kenny, access to information has been everything. "Ten years ago, you would had to rely on magazines and TV shows to know what was on in the international music scene. Micheal Jackson was all that people knew. And now, any conceivable music you want is just a 'google' away. At the same time, it has made everything so short-lived. There is no curiosity or patience left any more. We want instant answers." Copying things is easy but Kenny says that sooner or later one is invariably found out. Playwright Mahesh Dattani admits that he cannot do without Google at all. "It's invaluable as far as I go. I back-up all my documents on Gmail so that I don't have to carry a pen-drive while traveling," he says.

Google has transformed academics as well. Sociology professor Kamala Ganesh swears by Google for instant searches but always manages to pull up students whose assignments reek of copy and paste. "For scholarly assignments, Google is not too good. It is such a public space that you can easily get caught. Although I insist that students not take Google as the gospel truth, I admit there's no doing without it."

The addition of the verb 'google' to Merriam Webster (in 1996) turned out to be quite detrimental to the sale of the dictionary . "No one needs to buy a dictionary since then. The sale of reference books is on a decline," says Kenny.

Travel, too, is just a click away. Yogi Shah of Backpacker.co.in has introduced many to the wonders of seeing the world on Google first. "Even if you're staying at some place like Shimla Inn, you can spot it on Google Earth. The world is really at your fingertips."

Heading: Khan Do - Indian Express
Content: The truth is that we were waiting for Harman Baweja. The actor was scheduled to fly in for a function and we were on our official 'chowkidaari' at The Taj Chandigarh. He didn't turn up, but here's the twist - something, err, someone better, way better, walked in. Jackie Shroff, back in the city, in his charming best. "This time, it's a personal stop," he was in town for Abhinav Bindra's bash. A friend of the family, Shroff was all praises for Bindra the Champ, "non arrogant, decent, underplayed, respectful.....he's set an example." In fact, Shroff's son Jai, too is a sportsperson. His game is basketball. "And it will be the proudest moment when he makes it to the National team." In the meantime, acting is totally ruled out. Quiz Jackie about the latest developments, and he growls, "Mumbai? Bombay is dying," he laments how the city's become filthy and he'll soon take to the hills. "Khandala, where I'll do my farming," he steers clear of the potholes, jams and pollution. Looking forward to his films including Sai Baba, thrillers Ek Second and Chehre, Kisan and one in Marathi which is Renuka Shahane's directorial debut, Tiger's not interested in standing under the limelight for long. "I'd rather be a social worker," he's planning to open an orphanage and an old age home in the hills. Which reminds us, the actor has been active in short films too, particularly on issues which concern thalassemia, free education for poor children, and has made one for the UN. "Till you don't instill the fear factor, people will continue neglecting polio drops, AIDS prevention et al," feels Jackie, checking his notepad constantly. "I'm a net junkie," he never travels without his laptop. "Architectural sites, environment solutions, fashion, health, NGOs, art...surf's definitely up," he clicks on.

Heading: Amazing Amethyst - Indian Express
Content:
What's the first thing that comes to your mind as you hear of Cuba? A cigar is perhaps your first answer followed by its capital Havana. But there's more to the country than that. "There's a Cuban culture that involves a lot of singing, dancing, clubbing and of course there's our world famous rum," lists out Yusmel Gonzalez, the band manager of 'Nu Havana', a band that's been put together by the Cuban Ministry of Culture and is currently on a three-week, five-city tour of India to promote Havana Club, a Cuban white rum that's also now available in India. For the uninitiated, Cuba is known as a Bartender's Mecca, for here originated the Cuban National Cocktail – the Mojito.

But you don't need too many of those to relish Nu Havana's music. Here they are: Percussionist Janet Trillo, musician Alexey Quesada, animator Sandy Marquetti and dancers Narjara Fuentes and Aldeliz Publes make-up the two-year-old band that has been performing across the globe presenting a mix of salsa, reggae, hip-hop and even jazz, all packaged together in Cuban style.

And the first India visit for the five-member band has been full of surprises. "The India that we get to see back home on television is so different," tells Gonzalez mentioning pictures of inundated rivers, poor people begging and glimpses of the Taj Mahal thrown in. "You know India and Cuba are quite similar in some ways. The weather's same and so are the beaches," the band manager saying mentioning their performance in Goa that saw the crowds truly appreciate their kind of music that's very "vibrant and participative" in nature.

"India changes with every city we go. Truly there's so much diversity here and I would have loved to actually stay on and see more," added Sandy Marquetti who apart from being the animator (in charge of vocals, we are told) is also an actor back home. "Our band is actually the coming together of five different individuals who bring with them their own uniqueness that can best present Cuban culture," explains Sandy introducing us to Alexey who plays the trumpet and has also been a member of various Cuban bands. So has Janet Trillo while the ladies perform for the Cuban National Ballet. Surprisingly, they are yet to release their first album.

"In Cuba there's a party on every day. Everyone's into clubbing and dancing...basically Cubans like to live it up," pitches in Gonzalez who finds some parts of India matching up on that front. But have they actually heard us? "In bits and parts. I quite like..." Gonzalez stops and ponders before digging into his pocket, opening up a notepad and reading out what he's written. "Punjabi!" he tells us. And we aren't surprised.

'Nu Havana' performed at Hotel Mountview on Sunday evening.

Heading: ‘The wind beneath my WINGS’ - Indian Express
Content:
Did you know that Liz Taylor enjoyed the adoration and attention of her husband so much that he handpicked amethysts to be crafted by Van Cleef & Arples merely to convey how much he loved Liz's legendry violet eyes! Feeling jealous? You don't have to be and here's why.

Amethyst originates from the Greek word 'Amethuskein' or 'Amethystos which means 'sober' or 'not intoxicated'. This mineral gemstone is the most fabulously transparent member of the macrocrystalline Quartz. Manganese impurities lend colour while iron controls the colour intensity. Though in its purest form, it is colourless. The coloured amethyst ranges from pale lilacs to deep purples. This pocket-friendly gem is globally available and is majorly sourced from Canada, Bolivia, Uruguay, Argentina, Africa and Brazil. South American amethyst leads in size and a better colour saturation are seen in those from Africa. Brazil contributes the famous pale coloured Rose-de-France.

Amethyst represents spirituality and ancient wisdom. For ages it has been valued for its mystical abilities and healing power as much as it is admired by jewellery lovers for its rare combination of an iceberg charm and understated sensuality. Ancient cultures wore amethyst amulets as an antidote for poison. It was believed to prevent intoxication and so the Greek carved exquisite wine goblets out of it! Leonardo Da Vinci believed amethyst to dissipate evil and sharpen intelligence. Fine amethysts feature in the British Crown Jewels. The likes of Russian Empress Catherine the Great graced the amethyst connoisseurs list. One of the largest cut amethysts in the world weighs 343 carats and lies with The National History Museum, London.

The amethyst palette, available in large range of calibrated shapes and sizes, effortlessly adds élan to most jewellery forms. Let it be an Indian narrative enamelled piece, a geometric western design and even an abstract filigree piece of jewellery. Rose-de-France truly justifies the well-crafted Victorian jewellery. The richer purple hues deserve a royal salute for boldly beaming in plain collets as both rings and earrings. Visualize a chinnon saree in lavender and make a statement with a neckpiece in amethysts and diamonds. Team your plain blue/ pink/ gray/ maroon silks set in rich purple brocade borders with amethyst set in yellow gold reflecting Indian design sensibilities and you can't go wrong.

It's time to raise a toast to the rich hue and go vintage this season best captured by Just Cavalli's winter 2008 collection and Nine West for footwear both in leather and patent. For a more subtle look, one may play up the jewellery with frames and scarves by D&G. Back home one may opt for the minimalistic approach of Namrata Joshipura or the opulent combinations by Rohit Bal. And if you still doubt the royal quotient, remember Akshay's purple throne in 'Sinngh is King'. So let the lush lilacs and lavenders in. Before I wind up, please do not try and clean amethyst jewellery at home since it is highly sensitive and becomes pale with exposure to sudden temperature changes and strong chemical exposure. A professional shall also keep the setting technique in mind.

The writer is a city-based researcher specialising in jewellery art and can be contacted at sameeraahaan02@gmail.com

Heading: Snapshots of glory - Indian Express
Content:
The turmoil is evident. Both inside and outside. Blasts creating an unrest nationally, the want for power forming its nest of insecurity in the mind and the unjust social pressures eating up the system...amidst the chaos, we've neglected the basic: "The plight of the building blocks - women, the today and tomorrow of our society," says Anandmurti Gurumaa, as she greets turns the pages of her book 'Shakti, The Feminine Energy'. It was at the book launch in Panchkula that we got to go beyond the cover. "This is a tribute to women and will help the them discover the power and grace within," says Gurumaa, who feels that despite the 'modernism', women are still not enlightened enough and are mentally, physically and intellectually dependent.

"They still have a long way to go. They need to walk the path of self healing and should understand that they have a right to live life their own way." Women, she feels, need to stand up and voice out their rights and expand their horizon to achieve holistic fulfillment. "And for this, she needs to be educated, aware, have the ability to make decisions," Gurumaa's remedy lies in yoga, meditation and chanting mantras, not for God, but for the self. "For they have the precise structure to heal the mind and build on concentration," Gurumaa reveals the secret to inner peace.

Talking about the inherent power of women and the misconceptions conditioned by the society, the men, she reflects too need to undergo a change of perspective. "Rather than asking women to dress in a particular manner, men should change the way they look at her. Instead of suppressing her thoughts, men should just concentrate on their own," this, she says, is for the benefit of the man. "A free mind makes for a happy woman and a happy woman, a happy family," her logic is crystal clear. Stability of the mind is of utmost importance, she asserts.

Switching from subjects as varying from Zen, Sufi, Upanishad, Buddhism, to bard sages, philosophy, art, history, and yoga, Gurumaa speaks to the modern mind using ancient wisdom such as the vedas, sufism, and Buddhism. "Upanishads hold answers to today's problems and states what we need to do today -- give the lady her wings and let her be free and see the nation progress with her."

Heading: Devoted to the cause - Indian Express
Content:
Progressive Photographers Association celebrates tourism with captures of the city and other tourist destinations

The season of festivals has come knocking and thanks to World Tourism Day on September 27, the celebrations have begun early. And as a part of the same, the Progressive Photographers Association commemorated the occasion with exhibits of how they see the City Beautiful and some other popular destinations around. On display are different perspectives and 54 photographs by Harwinder Singh, Ashok Saini, Deepak Arora, Rajesh Kumar, Rakesh Dogra, Vipin Kumar, Sanjay Kaushal, P K Gautam, Deepak Rana, Deepak Arora, Nagendra Sharma, Arvinder Singh, Surinderpal Singh.

'The Other Side of Wonder' provides a rare riverside view of the Taj Mahal. The lights of puja at Haridwar in 'Lights of Enlightenment' form beautiful patterns in the river. A tourist couple on Punjab tour in 'Refreshing Toughness' encourages the photographer to go on. 'Fountains of Joy' and 'Snowfall in Chandigarh' are interesting captures of the fountains at the Rose Garden. 'Journey Back to the Real World' provides a clever contrast of a modern vehicle with the backdrop of ancient traditional structures untouched by industrialization. 'Salute' captures the play of light on black stone of the War Memorial and 'Good Morning' becomes the perfect Vastu object with its composition of the beautiful red-spread of the early morning November sun at the lake. 'The Light's Playground' is an unusual take on the passages of the Rock Garden. The silhouette of Haryanavi folk musician with his wind instrument rules the frame of 'Pied Piper'. 'Enjoying Balance of Poverty' presents a contrast of celebrations. A boy finds himself in the 'lap' of the Open Hand at the lake in 'Perfectly at Peace'.

On at Punjab Kala Bhawan till

September 29

Heading: Saturday night is here - Indian Express
Content:
Come Navratri, and the festive mood shows up in a more energetic manner and the outcome is a lively show of Dandiya. Imagine the dance form and colorful attire; coordinating feet and above all thumping beat come to your mind. So what is the music this Navratri?

According to Atul Jain, president Jhankar group who has been organising Dandiya for the past six years, "More than the music, it is the beats that are more important in Dandiya. In fact, Pune wants a mix of Gujarati, Hindi and I must say that that is due to the cosmopolitan culture that the city represents." Jhankar group has organised a dandiya night on October 8 at Gandharva lawns, Katraj.

There are a number of groups that invite DJs for performances but nothing can be as euphoric as a live music band making the dancers sway on their traditional Gujarati music. What is an added advantage of the live music band is the on the spot improvisation that is dependant on the liking and the category of the dancers. Jet set band and orchestra is a band of veteran musicians that has been winning the hearts of rock music lovers and dandiya and film music enthusiasts for years. Jet set is already ready with their paper work for the dandiya nights. Booked for all the nine nights, Eardley De Souza, the drummer of the band says, "We have been performing at dandiya since past 20 years and I must say what sells during dandiya is traditional Gujarati music. Keeping the beats factor constant, we go on improvising the music according to the age group, tempo of the crowd and the organisers' demands. For instance, for youngsters, the beats are faster. With elderly people we play more of traditional music. The energy of the crowd is also important while playing the music in garba." With five members from the same family performing on the stage, the band is one of the most popular and in-demand bands in the city.

The Melody makers, one of the oldest bands in the city, however, has a different opinion. According to Ashokbhai, member of Melody makers, "We play a mix of old and new songs. Raas, garba, Gujarati music and rhythm are all a part of the kind of music that we play. We can say with our experience that every year has its own trends and this year as well tracks like Darde disco, Dil mein baji guitar and other recent ones will dominate the music scene in dandiya."

With variety of music ready to entertain, the masses can be sure that they are going to have a gala time. Niharika Chawla and her friends are regular participants in the garba nights in the city and she says, "I love the grand gathering that garba is. The music is one of the most important factors in dandiya because all these gatherings and fun times spent with friends become memories because of the music. And every time that you try to recall them, the beats of garba are always present in the background."

Dandiya beats can make any soul sway, say bands that are going to perform on forthcoming dandiya nights

Some tracks this dandiya

* Darde disco

* Bachan ae haseeno

* Dil mein baji guitar

* Tune payal jo chankayee

* Hey naam re sabse bada

* Pankheda re - Gujrati

Heading: Love and longing - Indian Express
Content:
This could easily be called a post-Rock On effect. At least seven bands, comprising budding musicians from the city, got together to perform on one platform pouring out the best of their music for the young crowd at Sayaji Baugh Amphitheatre on Saturday night.

The organisers, however, said that with Vadodara being the cultural hub of Gujarat, the need to create a common platform for budding musicians was very much there, much before the release of Rock On.

"We realised that the city needed a common platform for young musicians," said Harsha Rajkonwar, one of the organisers. Over the last one month, Harsha and his friends have been busy talking to seven bands, while also rehearsing and improvising their own drumming skills.

On the other hand, posters and publicity were handed over to a motley group of students and artists from the Faculty of Fine Arts. "All of us here have one common cause — music. One doesn't need a lot of cash to arrange a programme of this sort, which has been happening in various pockets. All we needed was a little help from friends," he added.

With a modest budget of about Rs 15,000, Harsha and his friends roped in seven bands and musicians from the city on a Saturday evening. Just before the start of the event, he said excitedly: "We are expecting at least 300 people to show up. With the help of word-of-mouth publicity, social networking sites in the Internet, we posted messages to everyone we knew."

The posters and banners came later, as on the eve of the event, M S University's Fine Arts students conjured an image of plugs, mikes and switches to represent the theme of the show — And…Plug.

Much above expectations, at least 400 people came on Saturday evening as the newly formed band — The Banana Planters — doled out peppy numbers enthralling the audiences.

Saptak, a fusion-alternative band, dished out mellifluous numbers with just two acoustic guitars. On the other hand, the growls of Undergods and Lexium, a school band, captured the fascination of young school students donning black T-shirts. Phun Intended and Manefus revisited the grunge era getting audiences on a groovy high.

The high point of day however, was Boundless Spirit, comprising Bunny Bhargava, known for his poetry and Dylanesque numbers. Siby Abhimanue played their original songs taking the audience to a different plane.

Heading: Talking point with  Baba sehgal - Indian Express
Content:
Miley Jab Hum Tum

Star One

Monday to Thursday, 9 pm

Rating**

What's it about?

 Life in Excel College, throbbing with teenage energy and charm. Since love rules the heart and mind at this stage of life, the storyline is replete with crushes, flirting, heartbreak and longings.

Who is in it? In this fictional hippest college of Mumbai, Diya sashays down the corridor showing off her diva-like persona. This is enhanced by the constant presence of loyal Annie, who idolises Diya, and stupid Chacko (Doesn't this just remind you of Kareena Kapoor as Poo in Kabhi Khushi Kabhi Gham? Only sour point is lanky Diya lacks any of Kareena's attitude and oomph). Diya is shocked when her small-town cousins—shy and intelligent Gunjan and full of life Nupur—from Morena come to Mumbai. Diya's eyes are set on cool and stylish Samrat, who wins hearts as well as basketball matches. Though he is often caught flirting with Diya, Samrat is still waiting for that special girl. Samrat faces stiff competition from intelligent Mayank when it comes to wooing girls.

What's hot? The title song of the sitcom, meant to draw young audience, has a peppy feel. It manages to build up the mood with all the major characters making appearances in it. It offers the promise of a nice candy-floss drama unfolding in a Riverdale kind of setup. Though the starting episodes have not quite kept that promise, it remains to be seen whether the characters and scriptwriters pull up their socks to deliver a TRP-booster.

What's not? The storyline, a mish-mash of a number of teeny-bopper lover stories and college romances, desperately needs some freshness and original ideas. That's what had worked for Remix, a series set in a school, which was aired by the same channel a few years ago, or the hugely popular Hip Hip Hurray. Being little more careful while deciding the getup of the characters can also help. We also don't mind emphasis on acting than wearing off-shoulder dresses or tight salwar-kameez. And please, those cheerleaders and convertibles don't belong to a Mumbai campus. Will someone also tell Nupur that Mumbai is not the city where people come to meet the man of their dreams.

Should you be watching it? Yes, if you are the kind who clings on to college memories as if it's the biggest solitaire in your jewellery box. So recommend to the tribe who love to see repeats and rip-offs of Kuch Kuch Hota Hai or Kabhi Khushi Kabhi Gham.

Heading: Blast does not spare children: 10- and 11-yr-old among critically injured - Indian Express
Content:
Best fit
For Amit Tandon, playing the character of the NRI Abhay Singh in Saath Saath Banayenge Ek Ashiyaan on Zee TV was an easy task, because of his Canadian origin and the firang accent he sports. But after a successful run, Tandon has decided to call it quits. The channel has subsequently roped in Salil Acharya as a substitute in the show. Salil who has been a part of popular shows like Yeh Meri Life Hai, Kasauti Zindagi Ki, Kyunki Saas Bhi Kabhi Thi, Kittu Sab Janti Hai and Kasturi, is very excited about the role he has bagged. But matching Tandon's American twang is going to be difficult.

Sob tale
THE team of Golmaal Returns—Ajay Devgan, Arshad Warsi, Tusshar Kapoor, Shreyas Talpade and director Rohit Shetty—made it to the sets of Zee TV's Sa Re Ga Ma Pa to promote their latest venture. But it was Pakistani girl Sara Raza Khan's sob story that was the highlight of the show. The poor girl narrated a sordid tale of how she is being treated as an outcast here amongst her peers in Challenge 2009. This young girl who is away from home, in this metropolis of Mumbai, is actually facing a lot of objection from her people back home in Pakistan. While this definitely left everyone flabbergasted on the sets, we just hope her situation improves.

Home grown
NEENA Gupta has her plate full these days. After her much talked about wedding with Vivek Mehra, Neena is now resurrecting her career. She will make a comeback with her character of Manno Bhabhi in Saath Phere. She has been given the liberty to design her costumes, jewellery and hairstyle. Interestingly, the lehenga- cum -saree that she plans to drape in the show has been inspired by her costume that she had worn in her mehndi-sangeet ceremonies. We'll keep our fingers crossed.

Heading: No breakthrough yet, police probe the role of Bangladesh nationals - Indian Express
Content:
"I love all the songs of Sinngh is King and had gone to get a VCD of the film," says Vikas, the 10-year-old victim of Saturday's blast.

"He is least interested in studying and always craves for more and more CDs," says his mother Kailasho. Saturday was a holiday. So Vikas decided to catch a film and had gone to get a CD of his recent favourite when the blast destroyed his plans.

"There are injuries in my stomach and I was operated upon yesterday. I will be fine soon," says the boy. He has difficulty breathing and doctors have made him slip on an oxygen mask.

"Vikas is under observation," said Dr Manish Singhal at the AIIMS Trauma Centre. A resident of Mehrauli, he is the youngest of six. His father, Raj, works as a sweeper with the Municipal Corporation .

According to doctors at the AIIMS, six patients were operated upon on Saturday, of whom four are in a critical condition. "Two are relatively stable and have been moved to the ward. They are still under observation," said Dr Subodh Garg.

Sheetal Rawat (11) a student of Class VII, was returning from school with her mother when the incident took place. She too, has also undergone surgeries. Doctors say her condition is critical. "She is in the ICU," said Dr Singhal.

"The doctors have operated on her face, which was badly injured with her upper lip ripped apart, a fracture in the jaw and her tongue cut in half by sharpnels. A splinter is still lodged in the nape of her neck. But doctors say she is too young to undergo so many surgeries at once. They will remove the splinter later," said her mother Pratima.

Two of the patients who suffered brain injuries are in a critical condition too.

Another patient is 35-year-old Gyanendri from Ghatorni. The woman, suffering from fever, had gone to see a doctor in the nearby dispensary with her friend Kusum Chaubey (40), when the blast took place. Chaubey, a mother of six, suffered severe injuries in her right thigh.

22-year-old Saqib, a painter, is another blast victim. "I had gone to buy gutkha when I suddenly heard a deafening noise, after which I fell unconscious," Saqib said. He had splinters under his ribcage and some injuries on his shoulder. He is the youngest of five brothers and lives in Islam Colony.

Rajendar (22), a rickshaw-puller, was looking for a passenger when the blast occurred. "I just remember a deafening sound and then being taken to the hospital," he said.

His brother Raju, who works at a shop in the market, rushed him to the Safdarjung Hospital.

Shrapnel had to be removed from Rajendar's chest and on Sunday he was shifted to ward no 25 at the hospital. Dr Rajiv Krishna, the attendant doctor in the ward, has confirmed that he is now in a stable condition.

(Reporting by: Geeta Gupta, Mahender S Manral, Aneesha Mathur, Akshay Kumar V, Pallavi Jain)

Heading: September 13 serial blast toll now 25 - Indian Express
Content:
A day after the blast in Mehrauli's Sarai market, the Delhi Police are yet to find any specific clues about perpetrators. A child has died and twenty-two have been injured.

Officers of the South District Police said they have registered an FIR and are probing the role of some Bangladeshis, who could be behind the blasts.

Already, around 50 Bangladeshis have been interrogated and 15 detained. The police are probing the role of the two — Yessin Muhammad and Muhammed Majruddin — who were arrested from Jalpaiguri this July and are currently in Tihar Jail. Mobile phone records of some Bangladeshi nationals and other criminals are also being checked.

Suspicion of the involvement of Bangladeshis cropped up in view of the earlier blasts in South Delhi. The blast is the ninth there, for which no terrorist outfit has laid claims. Even though they had not caused much damage, the blasts in Hauz Khas, Malviya Nagar, IIT and Lado Sarai were executed in the same manner.

The explosive materials used in the low-intensity chemical-based bombs were quite similar and nails were used in earlier bombs too.

"Last month, a Bangladeshi was arrested for making the type of bombs which was used yesterday and later six crude bombs were recovered from Jalpaiguri on his tip-off. A team has been sent there for further clues," a senior officer said. Asked about the involvement of Bangladesh nationals, Joint Commissioner of Police, (Southern Range), Ajay Kashyap said, "I would not be able to comment on that front at present. We are investigating the case from every possible angle." Police sources said Delhi Police teams were sent to West Bengal's Jalpaiguri and Meerut in Uttar Pradesh after receiving some information in connection with the Mehrauli blast.

SKETCHES MADE
Sketches of the two men travelling on the bike are being prepared based on three eyewitness accounts. Police are probing the role of one Mohammad Ansar, who was allegedly residing in Delhi till sometime back.
His name had cropped up after the previous blasts too, but he is yet to be traced. His links with terrorist outfits are yet to be established as well.
The FIR in the case has been registered under Sections 302 (murder), 307 (attempt to murder), 427 (mischief causing loss or damage), 120B (criminal conspiracy) of the Indian Penal Code and Sections 3,4 and 5 of the Explosives Act.

RAIDS CONDUCTED
Several areas across the Capital, primarily in South Delhi, were raided by Delhi Police on Sunday. According to police sources, raids were conducted in Sangam Vihar, Madan Gir, Ambedkar Nagar and Mehrauli. At least a dozen people were detained for questioning. "Nothing concrete, however, has been found yet," a senior officer said.
Some suppliers of chemicals like potassium nitrate and sulphur have been approached to get details of recent purchases.

Few leads
Though a man was detained on Saturday night for allegedly sending an SMS to the Delhi Police, which read "Save Delhi if you can", the police still are not sure about his involvement in the blast.
A senior police officer said: "Nanak Chand, who was picked up from Gurgaon, had sent the SMS. He took a new SIM card in the name of Ramesh Chand from a mobile shop owned by one Kishan. He is being questioned as to why he sent the message. But nothing concrete has come up yet. Further questioning is on." Nanak Chand is a native of Aligarh.
On Sunday, two men were reportedly picked up from Faridabad for allegedly sending a hoax e-mail to the Faridabad police. The mail said that blasts would occur in Sector 15 of Faridabad.
The detained men were identified as Jatin Gaur, a BTech student of a private institution in Faridabad and Sunny, who had allegedly sent the e-mail.
But after interrogation by the Delhi Police, it was found that the men had no connection with the Mehrauli blast.
Ganesh, the owner of a Pulsar motorcycle, similar to the one used in the blast, detained from DLF last night was released after interrogation. "We detained him as his bike was found abandoned in the DLF area," the officer said.

Heading: Lessons in ethical hacking — now at your neighbourhood computer school - Indian Express
Content:
The death toll of the September 13 serial blasts in Delhi rose to 25 on Sunday as another vicitim, 22-year-old Tahir Ahmed, died at Ram Manohar Lohia Hospital around 1.30 pm. According to doctors, Tahir was in coma after being injured in the Barakhamba blast and finally succumbed to brain infarction (brain stroke) on Sunday.

"Tahir was comatose ever since he was brought to the hospital with severe head injuries and multiple splinter injuries all over his body. Despite our best efforts, he did not respond even once to treatment," said Dr S K Sharma, the casualty medical officer of RML Hospital.

Tahir's family was allowed to visit him for one last glance before the doctors declared him dead on Sunday. "We are helping the family in any way possible. It is a Sunday, and hence postmortem is not possible. His body has been sent to the mortuary at Lady Hardinge Medical College and the postmortem will be conducted on Monday. The body will be handed over to the family by noon," said Dr Sharma.

Tahir was a native of Jhansi in Uttar Pradesh and his parents wish to have his last rites in his hometown.

"Doctors had told us last week that my son was not responding to treatment and needed prayers more than medicines. We understand that doctors tried their best to save my son," said Zahir Ahmed, Tahir's father.

The family does not know how to take the body back to Jhansi, as RML Hospital does not provide ambulances. Social worker and president of the Sarojini Nagar Mini Market Association, Ashok Randhawa, who has been helping blasts victims after the 2005 blasts in Sarojini Nagar Market, is now helping the family arrange for an ambulance to take Tahir's body back to his hometown.

Tahir used to work as an electrician and was staying in Mandawali in East Delhi.

After the blasts, he was admitted at the neurosurgery ward of the hospital's Trauma Care Centre.

Heading: Bend It in Paharganj - Indian Express
Content:
Till about a month ago, Sudeepto Ghosh of Rohini would switch on his computer at work only to find a new virus destroying his system. An employee with an online travel consultancy, he would be perplexed and angry.

"Finally, I began browsing the Net for information on hacking," says the 24-year old, who then found an institute offering certified courses in "ethical" hacking. He signed up for a three-month course, to find software professionals, government officials and even cops in the class. A month on, he is contemplating a career switch as a computer security expert.

With technology invading our lives, the friendly neighbourhood computer institutes have begun offering courses in data protection, security and ethical or "white hat" hacking. Most are recognised by the Ministry of Information Technology.

"Technology has come to India in a big way over the last five years — cell phones, Wi-Fi, CCTVs or even easy electronic transactions — and we have to deal with its problems. Security breach is one of them," says Ankit Oberoi (22), centre manager at Innobuzz in Pitampura, which offers a course in Certified Information Security Expert to about 160 students.

Most of the faculty members are in their early twenties, and tactfully claim that they were interested in hacking since they were in school.

Quick to clear the air, Praful Aggarwal (22) of the institute — who is training top cops and corporate employees — says the course does not teach people how to hack into other systems.

"We basically teach them how to protect themselves. It is not legal to allow hacking into real websites and e-mail accounts," says Aggarwal, who is also taking an MBA course.

Agrees Rishabh Mehta (23), a software developer at Aptech. "I cannot hack into anybody's system because I could be caught by the police, but I can secure my network at work," says Mehta, who has managed to inspire his colleagues to enroll for the course.

"Hacking is a hit-and-trial process and we have to be ten steps ahead when training people, many of whom don't know a thing about hacking. So we regularly attend boot-camps and read to update ourselves," adds Oberoi.

Hit-and-trial often means discussing and also brainstorming together in hacking communities, which mainly remain out of the picture.

Preferring to keep mum on his own hacking expertise and the "power" over most technologically-challenged mortals, Oberoi quotes Toby Mcguire in the movie Spiderman — "With great power comes great responsibility".

While a police officer in the Operations cell waits for his teachers to appear, Aggarwal concludes: "This our way of channelising our talent and helping others with something that we know."

THE COURSES
There are three courses recognised by the Ministry of Information Technology and the HRD Ministry:
* Certified Information Security Expert, Certified Ethical Hacking provided by the EC-Council and the Certified Information Systems Security Professional offered by a handful accredited institutes in the city.
* While each course costs between Rs 7,000 and Rs 20,000, students are expected to provide identity proofs and a clean chit from the district deputy commissioner and sign an undertaking not to misuse skills acquired. The Institute is allowed to provide information and help the police track the student in case any hacking is reported.

LAWS AGAINST HACKING
While experts call for more refined and specific laws on hacking, the IT Act 2000, provides for personal data protection under four separate sections.
* Of them, Section 66 imposes a penalty of imprisonment of three years or fine up to Rs 2 lakh or both
* The Personal Data Protection Bill was introduced in the Rajya Sabha in 2006. The law will provide protection for personal data and information of an individual collected for a particular purpose by one organisation and prevent its usage by other organisations for commercial or other purposes. It will also entitle the victim to compensation.
But the Bill is yet to be cleared.

Heading: Spice Route - Indian Express
Content:
A new website offers football fans a chance to play tournaments and a chance to join foreign clubs right here in Delhi

Football enthusiast Debasish Roy, 40, has been trying to find avenues for talented footballers to play for a while now. One fine day, while leafing through the morning newspaper he came up with the solution; to create a common platform where football lovers, either players, coaches or managers could get together and play football tournaments. After investing Rs eight lakh and many sleepless nights, he set up magicoffootball.com, a one stop shop for aspiring footballers, coaches, referees, managers and sponsors to come together to play the game. "I was manager for two football clubs, Media Soccer in Delhi and Tarun Sangha in Kolkata. I wondered how to tap potential players, who lacked in confidence and I wanted to get in touch with sponsors as well," says Roy, who describes his site as the "Facebook of football". Roy, however, has never played football beyond the walls of his school campus. He also runs a consultancy, Royal Solutions, from his Dwarka home.

The site has been operational for the past four months and a runaway success as far as Roy is concerned. There have been 35 tournaments organised across the world through his site (eight in Europe, 11 in Indo-China, two in Russia, seven in Latin America) and seven in Delhi alone with names like Aloo Baingan tournament, Paharganj Petrifiers and Auto Riders. Anyone with a love for football or an interest in the game can use this website. "All you have to do is log on as a member and click on the 'Join the tournament' tab and select your profession (player, sponsor, manager, physiotherapist, ball boy) from the list. You can give a name to the tournament, select the venue, time and any special requirements if need be. Any random person can log in and choose to join the tournament, says Roy. Since the site is still barely six months old the tournaments are organized between three-four teams with six players on either side, for 30 minutes vis-a-vis the usual format of 11 players and 90 minutes. "This is not a professional league. You cannot expect 30-something executives to be fit enough to last a 90 minute game," laughs Roy, who is now holding talks with schools in the city for similar tournaments.

The website has already registered decent success. Holding true to the site's promise that you can 'Work or play with a foreign football club within a year of registration', two school boys from Kerala , Baby John, 14, and Ramesh Babu, 13, were picked by two football clubs from Chelsea and Aberdeen, the UK, to play. Even Abhijoy Basu, 37, an Asian Football Confederation certified coach,who was struggling to find new projects, says the site helped him. "I registered three months back. Within a week, I got an assignment to coach some businessmen in Noida for a fee," says Basu, who works part time in a government job.
