Later, after a seminar, they decided to attempt it, emerging finally as more "responsible" citizens. "Initially we thought it is just about clicking pictures, but later it dawned upon each one of us that awareness of road safety is a major problem in our city," said Kayzin Daruwalla (12), a seventh grader from Walsingham House School.

Farzin Dastoor (12) from Bai Ratanbai FD Pandey Girls High School said that the association with the international programme was a great experience. According to her, it helped the team of young photographers distinguish between safe and unsafe pedestrian behaviour by chronicling the city's roads for three days. "We being the future of the country, it was a good learning experience," Farzin said. Recalling the field trips in the scorching summer to areas like Churchgate, Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus, Mahim, Chembur, etc, the kids say that only on Day One of the trip did they have to struggle with the sophisticated cameras.

Eighth grader from Campion, Aatush Kallyaniwalla, said: "Sometimes we mistakenly deleted so good pictures we clicked, but we enjoyed it all."

Most of the kids believe now that pedestrians and motorists hardly follow any traffic rules. "We saw pedestrians crossing the road dangerously, jaywalking, motorists halting their vehicle on the zebra crossings, and more," Kayzin observed. She added that the traffic police should come down heavily on such offenders.

For now, the photographs will try to make the roads safer.

Heading: Speaking Silence - Indian Express
Content:
If Ramzan, Navratri and Diwali blend anywhere, it is here in Dharavi's Kumbharwada

Seventeen-year-old Sheetal Dewaliya meticulously makes colourful designs on an earthen pot, using a mehendi cone. She is undeterred by the hot sun or the smoke emanating from the nearby bhatti (kiln). She has to finish 1,000 such pots before the Navratri festival starts on Tuesday.

For the several hundred families living in Kumbharwada in Dharavi, this is the season when business peaks annually. Heavy smoke rises up from a kiln as soft clay pots are fashioned out of mud, cotton waste fuelling the kiln to fire them into hard and durable pots, diyas, tea-lights and other knick-knacks.

Kumbharwada's maze of narrow lanes, buzzing with the seasonal activity, got their name from the large number of Kumbhars or potters who came to the city from Kathiawada area of Saurashtra, several decades ago. Since then, this central Mumbai slum, often called Asia's largest, has housed this little township that churns out thousands of pieces of earthenware every week.

And with three festivals — Ramzan, Navratri and Diwali — lined back to back in the coming days, these families are busier than ever.

"I have been making diyas for Navratri and Diwali for the past 40 years. We start our work even before Ganpati, as these diyas and pots take more than a week to dry. Then the designing work on them starts," says 45-year-old Ebrahim Yusuf as he fashions a diya from a lump of blackish clay on a slowly moving potter's wheel. Yusuf's family moved here in 1956 and since then has been involved in the business. Like him, the business is passed on from generation to generation in other families too.

Work gets difficult in the monsoon, say these kumbhars, since their wares are dried in the open. "We start our work on a small scale even before the monsoon. But it is very difficult as there is no place to dry what we create. Also, the kilns don't work properly owing to the moisture in the air. We really dread that season," says 50-year-old Lakshman Dewaliya. Interestingly, this Hindu family has been making kulhars, the little earthen cups that phirni, the must-have delicacy at Mohammed Ali Road during Ramzan, is set in. "Most people are surprised to find Hindu families working for a Muslim festival. But communal differences are hardly an issue in this place," says Dewaliya.

The cottage industry works hard to keep up with the stiff competition from modern ceramics.. "I came to this place nearly 30 years ago. I learnt the art from my father. Since I have come here I must have made tens of thousands of pots. But things have definitely changed now," says 60-year-old Vasaram Tank. "My grandsons wanted to move to other industries, as there is more money involved there. They tried their hand at various occupations, but realised that they can't quite take pottery out of them. So they now manage their jobs and their passion for pottery simultaneously, by lending a hand in the evenings and on off days." Tank says this is also good to keep the tradition alive.

With the festive season around the corner, and Kumbharwada attracting customers from across the world, it is definitely a happy time for these families. These families have few material comforts, but that doesn't daunt their industriousness.

Heading: Nayak ensures Kingfisher’s entertaining ways - Indian Express
Content:
At this 25-yr-old institution for the hearing impaired, the library is called Whisper, the café is named Decibel. The school itself is named after 1972 Sanjeev Kapoor starrer Koshish

What's the first image that comes to your mind when you think about a school for the hearing impaired? Many would conjure up images of a child and a teacher gesticulating to each other, using sign language.

At Koshish, however, you will find neither child nor teacher communicating that way. This private institution, which provides free education to the deaf, insists on building children's speaking skills, and enhancing their ability to lip read, also imparting a

sense of independence in the process. "We want to remove some false notions. These children can be taught to speak," says Dr Ajay Kothari, an ENT specialist, and founding trustee of Koshish.

Kothari started building on his dream of creating an institution for the rehabilitation of the hearing impaired, in 1983. After his friend, the late actor Sanjeev Kumar, suggested 'Koshish' as a name after the 1972 Bollywood hit, the first school was set up, with 30 students to begin with. Three schools later and several years later, the institution has grown tremendously.

"We now have a 20, 000 square foot centre in Malad with over 130 students," says Kothari.

Students at Koshish study up to the SSC level and are given free hearing aids, which would otherwise cost them Rs 22,000. They are also given vocational training in tailoring, screen printing, photography, public speaking, hair styling, along with classes in yoga, aerobics and martial arts. "The basic idea is to make them independent. They can get jobs, or start their own businesses. They also write an exam that is certified by the government. If they want to continue with college, we help with 50 per cent of their expenses," says Kothari.

Interestingly, every department in the Koshish campus at Malad (East) is associated with the aural. The gallery is called the Labyrinth after the maze of canals in the inner ear; the cafeteria is called Decibel, the library is known as Whisper, and the Audiology Department is known as Echo. The campus also houses a Child Behaviour Counselling Department, a Mental Trauma Counselling Centre, and a Deafness Detection Clinic.

"We started an inter-school cricket tournament three years ago, and appointed a past Ranji trophy player to come and teach the children. Now when they watch a match on the television, they know what is happening," says Kothari, also adding that the Maharashtra Government has now decided to hold the tournament at the state-level.

The students also enthusiastically celebrate every festival that comes up, including Janmashtami and Sankranti. "They even created a pyramid for the dahi handi, and we had also called a professional kite-maker to teach the children how to make kites. The competition required them to make kites of different shapes, ensuring that they would fly," says Kothari.

Celebrating their 25th anniversary, students from Koshish put up a show on Sunday evening. Kothari says that being deaf, the children have the beat inside their minds now, so when the music is turned down, they still dance in complete sync to the song.

"When you see that, it makes you wonder who is really deaf — us or them?" asks Kothari

Heading: Old hands give it a spin - Indian Express
Content:
Kingfisher Airlines may have missed the bus to final by a whisker when they went down to JJ Welfare Centre narrowly in a bitterly fought semifinal but they definitely proved to be most entertaining outfit in this season's Mumbai District Football Association (MDFA) Division V league. Rightly then, they also provided the league with the highest goal-scorer in Savio Nayak, who also won the best player of the year award. And for someone who doesn't consider football as his primary sport, Nayak's achievement is even more noteworthy.

"I am basically a hockey player and have represented India at the junior level. Football is simply a passion, and when my company decided to form a football team, I naturally signed up," said the 25-year-old striker, who finished the season with 14 goals to his tally. Nayak added that he was extremely disappointed that his team had to bow out via a penalty shootout, but is extremely excited about getting promoted to Division IV for next season. "It was heartbreaking to say the least, but that is sport for you. We had dominated the league during the early stages and were confident of prevailing till the end," he explained.

The lanky striker, who hails from Orlem in Malad, revealed how hockey still remains his main interest and he is looking forward to get hold of the stick again very soon. "We do have a couple of corporate football tournaments coming our way, but I can't wait to get back on the hockey turf," said Nayak. He added that he had gone to Qatar for a couple of years in search of greener pastures, before taking up a job with Kingfisher Airlines.

Team manager Jude Coutto said that he was extremely pleased with his team's third-place finish in only its second season in the MDFA league. "Our team is represented by people who work in various departments, and we come together generally on Saturdays for practice," he said. Coutto added that his jolly bunch, which has a majority who belong to the above-30 club, simply enjoyed playing football and were delighted when this opportunity came their way. "Our management also has been very supportive of us and we hope to continue performing this way," he added.

So come next season, the Kingfisher Airlines outfit will be looking forward to provide many more 'good times' in Division IV, and look poised to do so with their 'king' Nayak at the helm.

Heading: Sanket sparkles in thrilling victory for MG MO - Indian Express
Content:
JJ Welfare Centre paid a heavy price for a goalmouth blunder by their custodian, few minutes from the final whistle, as Little Master clinched the Mumbai District Football Association (MDFA) Division V title on Sunday with a 1-0 win at the St Xavier's ground in Parel. Devendra Parab proved to be the hero for the champions as he found himself perfectly placed to net in the winner. Both teams will now be promoted to Division IV for the next season, and will have to brace themselves for tougher competition there.

The final failed to live up to the expectations as both teams seemed too content on defence, and once the Colaba outfit broke the deadlock, JJ Welfare had a tall-order to overcome, which they failed to do in the end. Match-winner Parab, who himself hails from Panvel, said that his young teammates come from different parts of the city, and practice at Colaba. The third-fourth playoff encounter between Kingfisher Airlines and Sealiners proved to be much more entertaining as the former won 3-2 in what proved to be a nail-biting contest. Savio Nayak opened the scoring for Kingfisher, before Rupesh More gave his team a 2-0 lead. But Clectus Ebnezer brought Sealiners right back into the game with a fantastic goal. A defensive folly then led to Savio Nayak winning a penalty, which he converted easily.

Heading: Exuberance leaves a hole in punters’ pockets, claims Million - Indian Express
Content:
In a game like water polo, rarely one player can make so much difference between victory and defeat. But that's what Sanket Shinde proved in MGMO's nail-biting 13-12 win over hosts PM Hindu Bath to move into the title round of the GMAAA's floodlit Water-polo five-team league, held at PM Hindu Bath near Charni Road, on Saturday night. Sanket was not only their pivot, but also their attacking forward, who notched up 10 of the 13 goals that his team scored against hosts' 12.

Till halfway stage, MGMO appeared to be in driver's seat, leading 8-5 with Sanket scoring six of them. But in the third quarter, it was the turn of PM Bath boys, who went for an all out attack and reduced the margin to 10-9.

The deciding quarter proved to be action packed one. It looked like that hosts might emerge victor when they led 12-11 with just a couple of minutes to go for the final whistle. But first Ravindra Dhuri made it 12-all with a power-packed throw which beat hosts' goalkeeper. Then just before the final hooter, Sanket scored from a close range to clinch the tie.

The winning team will now take on the defending champions Central Railway, who blasted their rivals with consummate ease. They first routed Andheri Sports club 19-2, then thrashed Police 15-2 and drubbed hosts PM Hindu Bath 15-6 to remain unbeaten.

In the women's final, Sayali Gudhkar proved star performer in MGMO's close 7-6 win over hosts PM Hindu Bath to bag the honours. Sayali netted five of the seven goals, while for the hosts the Thakkar sisters, Rahika and Pryanka, shared the spoils with two goals apiece.

Heading: Better love than never - Indian Express
Content:
Who says too many cooks spoil the broth? In fact, they indulge our appetites with new and luscious menus

There are people in Mumbai who track changing menus with the same fervour as others track changing governments. It's a sin to miss a new menu, especially if you're part of the crowd that makes it to the chef's table. It's equally unpardonable if you're a chef and your table's not where everyone wants to be seated.

At Stax, Hyatt Regency, Chef Giuseppe Zanotti's new menu offers a culinary journey across Italy. It runs through Sicily, Emilia Romania, Liguria, Trentino-Alto Adige, Campania, Piedroni and Sardinia. "The menu is sprinkled with prominent flavours of Parmesan cheese, fresh herbs and olives. Tiger prawn carpaccio with zucchini stew and coral sauce and Grouper filet with potato timbale, oregano and tomato reduction are just two of the specialties offered," he says. Zanotti is back from a holiday in Italy, re-charged before he launches his new menu on October 1.

A few kilometres across, at the JW Marriott, change is brewing in Chef Stephen Doe's kitchen at the Asian restaurant, Spices. New Thai delicacies like Wok flashed lobster in black pepper sauce and Pongkaree, prawns in curry powder, red chilli paste and finished with egg drop are the highlights of the menu. "I recommend Soft shell crab tempura and Miso Black Cod Fish in Japanese fare. Usually we change the menu at least once a year but it is better to do so every six months. It keeps our team excited and inspired."

Chef Jun Hu's menu (at China House) spans traditional regional cooking in China. He draws attention to vegetarian bean curd pancakes, 'Kong Pao' king prawns with lantern chillies and cashew nuts, Wok-fried king crab with ginger, spring onions and Shaoxin wine, Wok-fried spiny lobster with black beans, garlic and Sichuan chillies, Wok-fried snow peas with garlic, Clay pot chicken with smoked bamboo shoots, bean curd and chillies and Sichuan tenderloin poached in chilli pepper oil and garlic.

At Indigo, Colaba, they smoke out the old before it gets monotonous. Their new menu, designed by Rahul Akerkar together with Chef Nitin Kulkarni, always has tongues wagging. For fear of running out of space, we cannot mention the whole menu but their Asian-Western fusion menu comprising Fenugreek pesto, Pumpkin mash, Tendli with peanuts and the Spicy plum-cured tandoori chicken, Broccoli, ajwain potato mash and ginger marmalade sound delectable. "It took us a month to design it. New menus are a lot of hard work especially since we change ours every eight-ten months. However, Indigo classics like Lobster risotto and Lobster bisque always stay put," says Kulkarni.

"Old delights such as Asian spiced barbequed chicken, Baked Norwegian salmon, Donburi and Japanse Udon noodles with black mushroom scallion and prawn continue to feature on our new menu as well," says Joy Bhattacharya, Executive Chef of Trident and The Oberoi, explaining that there is no excluding some old favourites. As for the new menu at Tiffin, he says, "We have sourced the best ingredients to provide a taste of authentic Japanese delights like Japanese breakfast, Tori Oyakodon, Donburi and much more."

Bhattacharya insists good ingredients make a better menu. Same goes for the fresh menu at Frangipani, Trident, where, "A few Mediterranean ingredients like zattar, sumac, relishes such as shankhaleesh and shakshouka are the things to watch out for." Certainly, with so many nouveau menus, do we need to cook up an excuse to venture out?

Heading: Wowing vinyl - Indian Express
Content:
After his laugh-riot The President is Coming, Anuvab Pal offers Chaos Theory, a tale of two Harvard professors finding love after 30-year-long friendship

Do you believe love is better late than never?
I believe in love better early, best very early, equally good in middle age and very welcome late. Basically, take it whenever you get it.

How do the dynamics change when friendship becomes love?
A collegial banter, understood rudeness, traded familiar insults, inside jokes, common friends and physical comfort guide close friendships-love, I think makes that guarded and wary and also insecure. There are, in addition, the notions of fidelity and commitments. Friends don't need that but if they end up spending a lifetime together, as Mukesh and Sunita do in the play.

Which factors in the play would draw the audience?
Those who have watched the play say they have had some sort of a relationship similar to the principal characters, Mukesh and Sunita (a lifelong romance without the realisation of it), so I'm assuming identification. And of course humour, conversations about literature, college lives, and the meaning of academia, great 80s music.

When you updated the script from a one-act play, what are the elements did you include to expand it?
The play was written in two parts. The first was a 20-minute scene of their lives over one evening. And the second was when you visited their lives over in important events through the 60s, 70s and 80s. Once the past scenes started coming together, the present seemed repetitive. And yet it was important for the present to reflect their banter, so the tough task was to balance a night of chat and scotch drinking with flashbacks of their lives while trying to push the plot forward. Full credit to Rahul Da Cunha (director) for seeing that in the play and actually bringing out the dramatic action.

Would write a sequel of Chaos Theory to show how they carry the relationship forward?
I don't think a sequel after Chaos will work because it ends where it ends. Otherwise it could keep going like Hollywood movies. No one would watch Chaos-The Dark Knight for example.

What next on your plate after Chaos Theory?
I'm thinking about a play about money, in the style of a David Mamet play. Actually I'm also thinking about a trilogy-one about money, one about politics and one about bureaucracy.

(Chaos Theory will be staged at Prithvi Theatre on September 30, October 1 and 2)

Heading: Chatterati - Indian Express
Content:
While his single Ride it climbs up the charts and wins awards in London, singer Jay Sean travels to Delhi to belt out some rhythm 'n' blues

Londoners might not know Kamaljit Singh Jhooti, but mention Jay Sean and everyone with a little bit of rhythm and some blues in the soul will hum Ride it, the hit single that is riding up the charts and winning awards. At his recent Mumbai act, the British-Asian singer, however, nonchalantly threw in a bit of rap in his otherwise melodic pop R&B. Oh, that was just for fun, he laughed. The 27-year-old performed at Elevate in Noida on the weekened, as part of Ray-Ban VH1 Global Music Xpress.

"The set list is a mix of my old songs and new ones. But what I love doing is to add something that people have not seen me do before, like rapping," smiles Jay Sean, who debuted with Rishi Rich and Juggy D in Dance with you in 2003 and went on to belt out hits such as Eyes on you. "Rishi Rich and Juggy D are good friends and it was a wonderful experience, but we all have moved onto our solo projects and are happy for each other's accomplishments," he says.

So when Jay Sean released his latest album, My Own Way, whose track Ride it has won the 2008 UK Asian Music Awards for Best Video and Best Urban Act, he did it under his own label 2Point9/Jayded.

"When someone else is putting money on you, it gets frustrating after a point when a lot of what you do is decided by them. So I trusted my instincts and 2Point9/Jayded was born," he says. He is the only artist his label has signed on till now, but he says with relief that he is flooded with demos.

After a brief interaction with Bollywood — his track Dil mera was part of Kya Kool Hai Hum while actor Bipasha Basu appeared for his song Stolen — he is ready for more and is in talks with Shankar-Ehsaan-Loy. "I'm a huge Bollywood fan. I love the way the films offer everything — emotions and comedy and music. I am really look forward to working with the SEL trio," says Jay Sean, who wants to bring here his experience of the West.

But how did Kamaljit Singh Jhooti become Jay Sean? "Well Jay comes from my last name Jhooti and my grandmother used to call me shaan which is where Sean comes from," he laughs. That is a little bit of West in his name as well.

Heading: Staging art - Indian Express

Showman

Heading: The life of objects - Indian Express
Content:
An ongoing exhibit makes interesting parallels between theatre and the canvas

Looking at a photograph of artist Tejal Shah suspended between two chairs dressed in Victorian garb and trussed up with rope, one can never imagine the kind of production that went into shooting this single frame-setting the stage

for it was nothing short of a theatrical production.

"We had gone to several flea markets in Paris looking for the right kind of chairs, eventually we got some on hire. The authentic shoes I got were two sizes small for me and I could barely walk in them. The two skirts I had put on did not help the matter and when the plank I was supported on broke, I feared the shoot would never take off," says the photographer and video artist whose black-and-white self portrait, titled Lethargy, is part of a larger group exhibition, Anxious, hosted at Galerie Mirchandani + Steinruecke.

According to art critic Gitanjali Dang, who has ghost-curated the show: "To create a parallel between Anxious and Peter Handke's

Offending the Audience (1966) is not hyperbolic. The show aspires to undercut the pristine gallery space and make viewers anxious and uncomfortable." With the permission of artists, the show creates 'shenanigans' to challenge a complacent art-viewing audience.

Works have been hung on the ceiling; the lighting is not luminous, making the ambience surreal. In addition, there is music to confuse and complicate. "Since installations are by nature interactive, paintings lend themselves better to creating a distance," explains Dang.

The parallels between art and theatre are constantly drawn by artists and theatre persons themselves—it is delightful when one as a viewer can spot those similarities with the naked eye or derive it from the work through an indirect route.

With performance-based art, the connection to theatre is almost direct. The artist or a chosen protagonist plays out a 'role'. The next level to the performance is where a photograph or the video art installation is used to document it.

"Theatre, especially experimental theatre in India, hardly has any support. It survives by the skin of its teeth," verifies Malani, whose videos Medeamaterial and City of Desires, is a perfect example of the marriage between performance and theatre.

Painter and performance artist Neha Choksi, who has often done collaborative works with theatre person Rehaan Engineer, is another example of an artist collapsing the boundaries between the two disciplines. Having shown twice at Project 88 the artist set up a series of intervention and participation in Who's in Town Anyway. Choksi's videos of migrants arriving in the city, is spliced with performances and actions by trained theatre persons and audience members.

The delightful short stories by Bhupen Khakhar, like Phoren Soap, may not have had audiences or even a staging but his art works are rife with the elements of theatre. The use of light is often dramatic, the personal narratives are played out with large helpings of humour and the protagonists were always addressing an 'audience' real or imagined.

In the case of itinerant painter Raja Ravi Varma he derived much inspiration from Parsi

theatre and some of his compositions, mostly frontal and with

dramatic light, have been dubbed theatrical by scholars like Gulammohammed Sheikh.

In fact if M F Husain were to be believed, "there is a bit of theatre in every painting".

Heading: What is Japonism? - Indian Express
Content:
City-based NGO brings back the pristine glory of Muller's oil painting

Works of art have been there to appease and mesmerise one into the very beauty of it making one revel in its splendour but it's time now for the admirers of art to express their love. And that is what exactly a city-based NGO did. Performing the dutiful role of an art lover city - based NGO- Institute of Research and Development in Oriental studies- Arms and Armours (IRDOS) recently restored an 80-year-old painting of the great painter- A H Muller.

"Pune has been an integral part of India's history and a number of organisations in the city are ensuring that the city continues to contribute to conserving the glorious past that we have had and we too wanted to contribute to the heritage of art our country has," expresses Varsha Rakesh, curator and chief conservator, IRDOS,

The painting, an antique piece is a property of Jyoti Raichand and originally belongs to the royal family of Jodhpur. The lady featured in the painting is Raichand's mother and the portrait was made by Muller 80 years back. According to Rakesh, "The painting was in a bad condition when we first received it on July 25. The canvas was torn, the paint layer had started coming off and the painting also had blooming- a technical term that means foggy blue layer on the painting."

The exclusivity of the painting is that the medium used in most of Muller's paintings is transparent watercolour but this is one of the very few paintings in the country that is done using oil as the medium. Muller who was born in Kochi, Kerala finished his graduation from the Madras School. During the First World War, because of his part-German descent, Muller was asked by the British government in India either to remain interned or to join the volunteer reserve force. He joined the reserve force and won admiration for his lively sketches and drawings. After 1928, he was employed as the court artist of Maharaja of Jodhpur. The painting also reflects the characteristics of Muller's style like the influence of Roman figures and so on. It also has Muller's signature on it.

Explaining the treatments done on the painting Rakesh says, "In a two month treatment on the painting the IRDOS experts have done a number of treatments. The first challenge was to prevent the paint layer from coming off. It comes off due to the loss of medium over years and we have to restore the medium on the painting. Other processes include straightening, cleaning and so on."

The painting is now restored completely and the researchers claim that if proper care is taken the painting can be preserved for years.

Heading: Culture vulture - Indian Express
Content:
Naturally the first thought that comes to one's mind when hearing the word Japonism is that it has something to do with Japan. One would not be entirely wrong in that assumption, except that the word originated in France. It was first used in 1872 by author Jules Claretie, to describe the influence that Japan had on the Impressionist and Post Impressionist painters like Edward Manet, James Tissot, Toulouse-Lautrec and Vincent Van Gogh.

Some may argue that it was larger reflections of the increased trade of Japanese goods like vases, screens and kimonos, among the European gentry. The masters of the Edo period often known as Ukiyo-e artists began to be known in Paris as collectors, writers and critics sailed off to Japan in the 1870s. They brought back with them, prints and curios that created a taste and influence.

However it was more than a mere reflection as some artists, like Van Gogh went on to embrace some of the stylistic features of Japanese art its calligraphy and colours.

It was however a short-lived experiment for the painter and it never really pervaded or became a permanent fixture in his art.

Later however artists like Gustav Klimt incorporated Japonism as a painterly vocabulary in his art while Georges Bigot, even moved to Japan to study and imbibe the culture there. The fascination for Japanese culture can also be seen reflected in theatre in productions like Madame Butterfly.

It showed up in textiles jewellery and graphic design. Much later filmmaker Francois Truffaut made humorous comments on the fascination with Japan in Paris in his film Bed and Board where its protagonist Antoine (Jean-Pierre Léaud) has an affair with a 'Japanese beauty'.

Demystify art, e-mail georgina.maddox@expressindia.com
