Heading: CBSE stops student from taking exam at home - Indian Express
Content:
Two years on, the Panjab University is yet to decide the fate of Professor J S Dhanki, former chairperson of the Department of History.

An inquiry was marked against Dhanki in 2006 for allegedly tampering with the marks of students and awarding his daughter a better score. But even as the inquiry carries on, the university has re-employed Dhanki for one year after his retirement.

Vice-Chancellor Professor R C Sobti had constituted a committee to look into the matter, which submitted a detailed report to the V-C recently.

Professor Sobti told Newsline: "I have been unable to go through the report because of my tight schedule.

The report will be tabled in the Syndicate meeting next month and a decision will be taken then."

Meanwhile, Prof Dhanki's re-employment has also received criticism from faculty members.

A fellow said: "His re-employment is questionable and the university should have cleared him of all allegations first. It is a setback to the teaching community that anyone with a shady background can be given benefits by the varsity."

Earlier the initial inquiry conducted by Dr J C Bansal found that the marks of several second-year MA History students were reduced to declare Harminder Kaur, the daughter of Professor Dhanki, the topper. Prof Bansal's report suggested that Harminder had left certain easily recognisable marks on the paper and her answersheet was liberally marked by the examiner.

Heading: Lily Garden and the fight to preserve its lost significance - Indian Express
Content:
The future of Ganesh, a differently abled student hangs in balance, owing to the apathy of the Central Board of Secondary Education. In what can be termed as an example of indifference, the Board has failed to grant him permission to take his Class X Board examination from home. With the last date to submit forms having lapsed on October 1, Ganesh is a worried person.

Ganesh, is 100 percent disabled since birth, and wanted to appear for his Class X examination as a private candidate. "After facing rejection from more than 40 schools, I requested the CBSE to grant me permission to appear in the exam. I also wrote to the UT Administrator, General S F Rodrigues (Retd) on whose instructions, the UT Administration represented my case," said Ganesh. He has, however, not received any reply from the Board yet.

"The last date for submission of forms is already over and I have received no intimation from the Board. If nothing concrete comes up, my one year will be wasted," he rues.

He added that the Board is harassing him and repeated enquiries have generated the same response of 'looking into the matter' from officials. His problem, however, has not deterred the boy and he passed his Class V and Class VIII board examinations in the first division from the Punjab State Education Board.

"Books are my best friends. My favourite subject is English and I aspire to be an IAS officer," he says.

Heading: Chandigarh Admn launches website dedicated to its smoke-free initiative - Indian Express
Content:
Given the place's historical relevance, it is surprising that few people in the city are aware of the Lily Garden. While the name suggests that it's a place where lilies bloom, it's anything but that. Tucked away in the heart of the residential area in Sector 9, it projects itself like any other garden with its cemented paths and towering trees.

There's nothing here — no boards or signages — to echo its importance until one stumbles upon a huge cuboid-like structure housed in the middle of the garden. Made from cement, it boasts of two dilapidated plaques that appear to have seen bad weather. The iron bar surrounding it, coupled with the thick undergrowth, make it difficult to examine.

A sharp eye catches the message on the black granite slab— "Jawaharlal Nehru, Prime Minister of India, saw the layout of Chandigarh from this spot on 2nd April in the year 1952".That, in a way vociferates the importance of the place.

Not very far away, another plaque, in an equally regretful state reads: "This memorial was inaugurated by M S Randhawa, Chief Commissioner, Chandigarh on 27th Februrary, 1967."

The Lily Garden indeed houses a memorial to Nehru's vision of planned urban development. Ironically, there's nothing that celebrates the importance of the place.

Interestingly, a hundred metres away, there stands a tower-like structure with huge iron frames bordering it on four sides. Again, there's no mention of what the tower is or its significance.

As one enters the area, one notices something missing. "There were plaques here too. See the missing spots. They've been gone for a long time," explains the neighbourhood dhobhi from across the street. What remains now are empty spaces with moss all over around the broken steps.

We turned to M N Sharma, former chief architect of the city, who had worked closely with Le Corbusier and M S Randhawa, former Chief Commissioner of the city.

"It's called Lily Garden?" questions Sharma as we quiz him on the place. "Is there a pond now? Did you go up the tower? There were wooden steps I remember," adds Sharma.

Recalling the day Pandit Nehru had surveyed the city, Sharma adds, "The tower had steps leading to it. It had four sides and Pandit Nehru looked around from each. This is a very important place for the city and needs to be highlighted."

Heading: Plastic is dangerous: Chief Justice - Indian Express
Content:
The Chandigarh Administration, in association with a local NGO — Burning Brain Society — launched a website — www.chandigarh.tobaccofreeindia.com — for a smoke-free Chandigarh initiative. UT Home Secretary Ram Niwas, launched the website at the UT Secretariat on Wednesday.

As a novelty, the website will contain a "violation reporting mechanism" wherein people can report any violation, which will then be directly routed to the police and the Health department. This online violation reporting mechanism is the first of its kind in the country and shall be useful to sustain the "smoke-free" initiative.

Chandigarh is the leader of tobacco control in India and this novel initiative once again consolidates its position as a leader in promoting health and the wellbeing of all citizens.

The officials of the Chandigarh Administration said Chandigarh is committed to ensure proper compliance with the law and do everything required to sustain the smoke-free campaign.

"This comprehensive website on Smoke-Free Chandigarh has been developed to spread awareness and disseminate information about the laws relating to tobacco control and smoke-free regulation," said Hemant Goswami, a member of the Chandigarh Tobacco Control Cell.

The website contains all the laws, rules and regulation; proper guidelines for all sections of people and businesses so that they comply with the laws and further the objective.

Chandigarh became the first smoke-free city in the country on July 15, 2007 and successfully completed the first year in 2008.

Till date, Chandigarh remains the only city in the entire country where all hotels, restaurants and educational institutions are smoke-free and there is a 100 per cent compliance by them.

Heading: Smoking in public banned from today, but what do the rules say? - Indian Express
Content:
"Don't sell polythene bags in Chandigarh. Sell it outside the city — in Punjab and Haryana — once the ban is imposed. Polythene creates havoc, it is an environmental hazard," Chief Justice Tirath Singh Thakur of the Punjab and Haryana High Court told this to the plastic manufacturing industries on Wednesday.

The Chief Justice refused to grant stay over the ban proposed by the Chandigarh Administration, wherein it has decided to make Chandigarh "plastic free" by October 2.

Appreciating the absolute ban on plastic by the Chandigarh administration, the Chief Justice observed: "We will not like to ban use of polythene by way of a judicial order. If the Chandigarh Administration decides to remove plastic from the roads of City Beautiful, why should we bring it back? We don't want to stay the ban. It is very well advised by the Chandigarh Administration".

Observing that polythene is dangerous for human beings, the Chief Justice said that polythene is unpleasant, unpopular and not bio-degradable.

Admitting the petition filed by few industries challenging the absolute ban over use of polythene in Chandigarh, the Chief Justice held that it was a serious matter.

"There is no organised method for collecting these polythene bags. The idea behind increasing the thickness of polythene bag in Delhi was to help the ragpickers, so that they can pick it up and earn some money by giving it for recycling," said Chief Justice Tirath Singh Thakur.

On the other hand, counsel for the industrialists averred that such an absolute ban on those units which are in the business of manufacturing plastic. The counsel further highlighted that a large quantity of eatables and milk products are supplied in plastic packing. "This is an experiment that the Chandigarh Administration wants to do. Let them try it. They might reconsider it as well," held the Chief Justice.

However, Justice Thakur asked senior standing counsel for UT Administration, Anupam Gupta to make alternative arrangements such as jute bags etc for packing of eatables and milk products.

Meanwhile, strongly advocating the move of "absolute ban on plastic", a reply was filed by Ishwar Singh, IFS, Director (Environment), Chandigarh Administration.

"The challenge to the ban is actuated and motivated purely by business considerations. The ban has been imposed by the Administration as a matter of conscious policy, in the interests of the present and future generations, in order to protect the environment and prevent its degradation and is eminently in public interest."

The changing lifestyle of the people and growing consumerism have added considerably to the pressure on the environment. An increased use of polythene bags is a part of this changing lifestyle. This is particularly true in the case of Chandigarh which has the highest per capita income in the country.

The ban on polythene is a conscious and considered policy decision to protect the environment and is both remedial and anticipatory in nature, reads the reply.

Heading: Two more behind bars, 1 at large - Indian Express
Content:
Come October 2 and smoking in public places and workplaces will be prohibited as per the directives issued by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare on May 30, this year. This empowers the Human Resource department of any organisation, to penalise and issue challans to its employees, if found guilty.

The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, on May 30, 2008, had issued the notification under the "Cigarettes and other Tobacco Products (Prohibition of Advertisement and Regulation of Trade and Commerce, Production, Supply and Distribution) Act, 2003.

According to the rules, employees and/or visitors shall not be permitted to smoke within the office which include staircases, elevators, lobby, passages, terrace and the parking area. The rules empower the HR Head, Branch Head, the Administration Head and/or the Legal Head of the organisation to ensure that no person smokes under his/ her jurisdiction.

Ashtrays, match boxes, lighters or other equipment designed to facilitate smoking, will not be provided at the workplaces and the manager of the establishment is liable to be fined for any violation of the prohibitory orders.

For smokers, the authorised personnel can approve and/or provide for a separately ventilated area called "Smoking Area", which will be situated in the basement area and/or any such area apportioned for such purpose.

Employees of a particular organisation, who smoke, are liable to dispose of, any material that remains behind after smoking, in specific bins provided for the purpose, on their own.

"Public places" have been defined in the Act. For instance, a "Hotel" shall mean a building or a part of a building where lodging, with or without board or other services, is provided by way of business for monetary consideration or otherwise and includes boarding house and guest house. "Restaurant" shall mean any place to which the public has access and where any kind of food or drink is supplied for consumption on the premises by any person by way of business for monetary consideration or otherwise and shall include the open space surrounding such as premises and refreshment rooms, banquet halls, discotheques, canteen, coffee houses, pubs, bars, airport lounge, and the likes.

"Open space" mentioned in Section 3(1) of the Act shall not include any place visited by the public such as open auditorium, stadium, railway station, bus stop/stand and other such place. "Public place" defined in Section 3(1) of the Act shall also include work places, shopping malls, and cinema halls.

The designated smoking rooms is defined as physically separated and surrounded by full height walls on all four sides; has an entrance with an automatically closing door normally kept in close position and has an air flow system with negative air pressure in comparison with the remainder of the building.

Heading: Pinjore-Parwanoo bypass on the fast track - Indian Express
Content:
Accused are drug addicts, cases of narcotics possession registered against them: police

Two of the five accused, who allegedly kidnapped a German national from Hotel Taj GVK and molested her on Sunday, surrendered in the district courts around 4 pm on Wednesday. The two, identified as Sukhwinder Singh alias Sukhi (23) and Maninder Singh Jolly (24), were remanded in police custody for two days by the chief judicial magistrate.

Of the five, 20-year-old Pankaj, was arrested on Monday while Harpreet Singh alias Dalli was arrested on Tuesday.

The last accused, Sompal, is still absconding. Jolly was the one who approached the victim first while Pankaj and Harpreet dropped her at Sector 20 later, said police.

Sukhi and Jolly surfaced in court today soon after Harpreet was remanded to two days in police

custody. Both had scratches on their arms and appeared with muffled faces. They were sent for a medical examination to Government Multi Specialty Hospital, Sector 16, late on Wednesday evening. Jolly suffers epileptic fits sometimes, said his defence counsel.

According to the Ambala police, both the accused are drug addicts and have several cases of narcotics possession registered against them. Reportedly, the duo is also facing trial in another case of kidnapping at Ambala.

In their statements to the police, Jolly and Sukhi said they came to Chandigarh on Saturday evening along with Sompal, Pankaj and Harpreet. They had drinks at a liquor vend in Kaimbwala village and then went to Hotel Taj "just to hang around".

Jolly told the police that they saw a foreigner standing in the parking lot and he went to talk to her.

"After a brief conversation about her name and nationality, the girl asked us to let her drive the Scorpio, to which we agreed. She sat in the driving seat and we all drove off from the hotel," said Sukhi in his statement to the police.

According to the police, after driving for a while, the girl got nervous and wanted to return to the hotel but the youth refused.

The accused kept mum when asked how the girl sustained bite marks and injuries all over her body.

Sompal, who is still absconding, is considered the most notorious among the lot by the police. He is facing trial in an attempt to murder case, said a police officer.

"Raids are on at various places in Haryana and we hope to nab Sompal soon," said a police officer.

Heading: Gagan on top - Indian Express
Content:
After weathering several delays, construction of the Pinjore-Parwanoo bypass finally started on Wednesday.

The residents of Bitna and Ghatiwala villages have accepted their compensation cheques, allowing the National Highway Authority of India (NHAI) to acquire around nine hectares of land.

The Rs 270-crore project, to be completed in two-and-a-half years, is part of the Zirakpur-Parwanoo four-laning project.

"The machinery had arrived months ago and we were waiting just for the land to be allotted to us. At present, we have possession of only 15 per cent of the total land to be acquired," said an official of Jaiprakash Associates, the company implementing the project on behalf of NHAI.

The officials had recently earned the Punjab and Haryana High Court's wrath for the delay in the acquisition process and the starting of work on the bypass. Interestingly, the land acquisition comes a day before the hearing in the ongoing case.

The proposed 11-kilometre bypass will have 15 bridges and five underpasses on the route.

"The bypass will begin from near the Malah road, go via Yadvendra Gardens of Pinjore and join the National Highway near Timber Trail in Parwanoo. It will pass through Horticulture Garden, Amar Palace, Bitna village, Tipra village, Kamli village and the fruit market in Delli village," added the official.

Heading: Sanjay has two much on his hands - Indian Express
Content:
Kuunal Lall has reasons to feel disappointed that a career that stole the limelight with his 2004 debut, ended just as abruptly at the age of 24. But the left-arm pacer is ready to move on, and step into the exciting world of Indian Cricket League. In a candid interview with Sportline, Kuunal speaks about the cold vibes in the Delhi dressing room, disappointment of being let down by his team mates and disadvantages of being a famous cricketer's son.

Your moving on to ICL is seen as a logical step, say following on your father's footsteps.
Yes it was a logical step for me, but not because my father was associated with ICL, it's more because of the way the DDCA treated me. I had an offer even last year to be part of ICL but I stayed back because I wanted to play for Delhi. It's very disappointing that a player who has played for you is treated like that. I have played with Vijay Dahiya (now chief coach of Delhi ) and it's very shocking when he turned his back towards me without any proper reason.

They got a player from Haryana, who even the state doesn't consider good anymore, and made him play for Delhi when I was fit. I did get a letter to join the one-day camp but I refused saying that I wasn't mentally ready — it took me some time to recover from the shock and humiliation my own team mates gave me.

Are you saying that there are problems in the Delhi dressing room?
Yes it was like that, the atmosphere within the Delhi dressing room wasn't right. I was part of the pace bowlers' camp but I felt like going through the motions. I was getting cold vibes from everybody, everyone in that dressing room looked to safeguard his own interests. So I decided to move on and be somewhere where I am respected and welcomed.

In hindsight, did you succumb to the hype of being a famous cricketer's son?
The DDCA and everybody around always saw me as Madan Lal's son, never as Kuunal Lall. They never saw what I was doing, my record of 41 wickets in 13 matches isn't bad but it never mattered to the DDCA. My only drawback was I got injured in between, but whenever I played, I gave my 100%. I was always in the limelight because I was Madan Lal's son. If I didn't do well in one match, the selectors began speaking about me immediately but wouldn't do for other people who haven't performed either. I have always gone under the scanner because I have a famous father.

Is this the reason you preferred not to play for Delhi Giants?
(Laughs) I was sick of Delhi, so I wanted to play for some other state in the ICL. I had a choice between Hyderabad and Ahmedabad, and I opted for the latter. Yes, my dad is coach of Delhi at present, but I wanted to create my own niche.

What are your objectives after joining ICL?
Everyone thinks ICL is just a cakewalk and it's easy cricket. It's not. The training I went through in the pre-season camp, I haven't experienced even at the first-class level. Also I am joining ICL because I have a point to prove and tell people of my abilities. I want to tell them that I haven't quit Delhi to join ICL because I wasn't good enough for first-class cricket, but to show them what I was worth of, that they ignored.

Heading: Are students allowed to smoke in hostels? - Indian Express
Content:
Even as the national selectors sat down to select the squad for the first two Tests against Australia, one man went about patiently observing and correcting the basics of youngsters at the Bharat Nagar Cricket Academy. Sanjay Bharadwaj may not be a name familiar to the cricket-obsessed nation, but for two members of the squad that was finally announced on Wednesday, the man is responsible for their journey to the national ranks.

Delhi opener Gautam Gambhir and leg-spinner Amit Mishra, who were named in the 14-member squad, both learned their trade under Bharadwaj in the city. With this, Bharadwaj has joined an elite group of coaches — alongside the likes of Tarak Sinha and Ramakant Achrekar — who have had atleast two of their wards in the national squad at the same time.

"I had achieved this distinction before as well, way back in 2003, when they were both given their first breaks on the Bangladesh tour. It has taken another five years for them to regroup, both of them had to go through different struggles all these years but I am happy they have come through," Bharadwaj said.

While Gambhir has made the opener's slot his own in all forms of the game — ODIs, Tests and even Twenty20 — Mishra has got his break now, and there is talk that he is being looked upon, again, as a possible replacement for Anil Kumble.

"Gambhir has established himself in the last one year, and I kept telling Mishra that his time too will come very soon. I told him that he will play for India again, and we had a friendly bet that he will play for India by October. By sheer coincidence, he's made it on the first day itself. He owes me a treat for this," he said.

Bharadwaj, however, admits that perhaps their respective approach towards playing the game also made a difference in their playing for the country. "Gambhir was very focused on playing for India right from the onset but Mishra was just keen on playing Delhi state so that he can search for a job and can settle down. I told him not to waste his talent like that and that he would for the country, but he didn't take me seriously. He always said laughed it off and said I was encouraging him only because I was his coach," he remembered.

But the man who is being credited for grooming youngsters in the Capital diligently is clear that his focus remains on his academy here. Bharadwaj, a qualified Level III coach, said he is not keen on pursuing more lucrative offers from other states.

"I have a dozen offers with me but I won't trade my academy for anything. This is my nursery where I groom talent, and I prefer keeping a low-profile. My job is to recognise and hone talent, and I will keep doing that," he signed off.

Heading: English-speaking beggars on prowl in Delhi streets - Indian Express
Content:
As smoking is banned at public places from today, university campuses across the country are set for a real testing time.

University authorities are yet to formulate a concrete plan on how to enforce the ban on campuses, which are "breeding grounds" for future smokers.

Institutes like the Jawaharlal Nehru University and the Delhi University in the national capital have banned smoking much earlier to the government's notification.

However, the effect of such measures are yet to be seen on the campuses.

"Delhi University had already banned smoking a year ago. But I find students smoking even in front of patrolling police personnel," said Sonia, a law student of Delhi University. "I don't think the ban by the Centre is going to make any difference on the campus," she said.

JNU Campus Development Committee Chairman Manoj Pant said the university has banned smoking in the academic complex, classrooms and libraries.

"After the ban from October 2, the issue is that whether students can smoke in the hostels," he said. "We will put out circulars everywhere and ban smoking in common rooms and games rooms. But we are not sure if the ban extends to the hostel rooms and it will be difficult to impose such a ban there," he added.

DUSU President Nupur Sharma appeared optimistic about banning smoking on campuses.

"Last year, we put a ban on smoking. So the fresh ban by the government will not make much of a difference. But now, anyone can be fined for smoking at a public place. This will make the ban more effective," she said.

As per the government notification, smoking is banned at public places such as hospitals, offices, educational institutes and libraries among others.

Heading: Shot on way home, cops hunt for clues - Indian Express
Content:
They come to you dressed in rags but will take you by surprise with their perfect accent and mastery of the Queen's language as you walk through Connaught Place in the heart of the national capital.

They are the modern English-speaking beggars who would not ask for money or food but will hit at your conscience by asking you to buy them medicines which they "badly need".

While some pay few rupees to get away, many got cornered by the "emotional blackmail" and would actually agree to buy the medicine provided they do it themselves.

And so, the beggars take their "unsuspecting victims" to the nearby chemist's shop from where they buy the medicines.

Overwhelmed by the feel-good factor of having helped their fellow men in need, the victims walk away with a clean conscience little did they know that they are duped.

"That's exactly how I felt. But somehow, I suspect later that something was amiss. When inquired, I found out that the shopowner has a tie-up with the beggars. Their modus operandi - the beggars brought back the medicine intact and get half the money of the cost price from the chemists," Ajit Dubey, a marketing executive and a victim of such a trap, said.

"I spent Rs 270 to buy one fellow an inhaler but later the guards nearby said the beggar usually makes a fool of foreigners by his sob stories and many even take out money from the ATM to give him," Dubey said.

Heading: Gout, civic body get HC rap for ‘not caring’ for dyslexic students in their schools - Indian Express
Content:
Over 36 hours on, police piece together one conclusion: robbery not motive

More than a day-and-a-half after Soumya Vishwanathan, a journalist with the news channel Headlines Today, was found shot dead in her car near Vasant Kunj late Monday night, the police, otherwise clueless, have come to one conclusion: robbery was, in all probability, not the motive.

The police are now depending on forensic evidence to crack the mystery death.

"Preliminary investigations suggest it can't be robbery," a police source said. "It could either be road rage or murder due to personal enmity."

Late Monday night, the police found Vishwanathan, 25, dead in her car — still on the driver's seat, the head reclined towards window on the driver's side. Doctors at AIIMS declared her dead on arrival; though police initially deemed it an accident case, the autopsy found a bullet lodged in her head.

On Wednesday, DCP (South) H G S Dhaliwal said, "We suspect two bullets were shot. A suspected bullet sign has also been found on the front number plate of the car. No sign of a bullet has yet been traced on the tyre, which had burst."

Dhaliwal said a country-made pistol (.315 bore) was seemingly used. He did not want to comment further on the investigations, saying only that all possible angles are being looked at.

Police officials involved in the probe said they suspect the shots were fired when both the victim's and assailants' vehicles were in motion, and at least one shot was fired after the latter overtook Vishwanathan's Maruti Zen.

The FIR (481/08), registered at Vasant Kunj police station says: "Front driver side glass is broken and there are traces of blood at several places in the car. Some hair was also found at backseat of the car.

"The car had climbed onto the divider and front driver side tyre was burst. Its rim was also damaged and there were skid marks at the spot."

The police on Wednesday afternoon sent Vishwanathan's car for ballistic examination at the forensic laboratory in Rohini.

About blue paint marks found on then journalist's car, DCP Dhaliwal said, "It could have been there before the accident. It may have come as the car was rammed into the divider, or it might have come from another vehicle due to rubbing."

More, he said, could be said once the forensic reports are out.

The police said Vishwanathan's family members were briefly questioned about the incident today; no statement has been taken from them yet.

QUESTIONS UNANSWERED
* How many assailants were there?
* What were they travelling in?
* How many bullets were fired?
* Where is the cyclist who noticed her first?
* Is police suspecting personal enmity?

Heading: Capital jitters: On road but left nowhere - Indian Express
Content:
Bawa Aditya Singh, 27, is a manager with a restaurant. He is dyslexic.

Singh is what he is today to a large extent because of the foresight of his mother Anjuli Bawa, who runs the country's first online website 'Action Dyslexia Delhi — Beyond Education' to help parents of children with learning disability. But Singh is lucky that his mother probed deep enough to learn more about her son's "fear of reading" — he was also the first student to get concessions from CBSE during his Board exams over a decade ago. But this is not the case for 22 lakh children in schools run by the Municipal Corporation of Delhi and the Delhi government.

On Wednesday, the government and MCD were left looking for answers when a High Court division bench of Chief Justice A P Shah and Justice S Muralidhar asked them if there was a prevalent mechanism to identify dyslexic children in government-run schools. The court found that the schools hardly kept any medical records of students.

"Dyslexia is difficult to identify unlike other disorders. Why are there no special or trained doctors to identify or help dyslexic students?" the Bench asked. "Imagine the state of these children if they are unable to cope with the mainstream."

MCD runs 1,800 schools; the state government runs approximately another 1,000.

"MCD has 67 full-time doctors plus nurses and assistants available for its schools; what are they doing?" the Bench asked. The court directed both MCD and the government to submit a detailed report on various disabilities detected among students — "class-wise, school-wise".

"One to two per cent children in every school in Delhi is severely dyslexic. Four to five per cent in every school has other learning disability," Dr Roma Kumar, senior consultant and clinical psychologist with Sir Ganga Ram Hospital, said.

But she said it would be impossible to spot a dyslexic child before the age of six or seven.

Defending the government, counsel Najimi Waziri said, "We do have specially trained teachers focussed on integrating special children into the mainstream. There is also a Disability Commission for Delhi to devise special schemes for such children."

Common symptoms of dyslexia
* Seeing words in 'mirror image', or reverse image — C as D
* Poor writing, spelling and numbering skills— 72 as 27
* Introvert nature
* Intolerant to critcism
* Preference for company of younger children
* Easily distracted and temperamental
* IQ usually average or above-average

Heading: Deathly half-hour: From 3.15 am to 3.45 am - Indian Express
Content:
The police: 500 Police Control Room (PCR) vans and 120 motorcycles patrol Delhi.

Delhiites: Simply not enough; most feel insecure.

Puroshottam Das, Deputy Commissioner of Police (PCR): "PCR vans patrol round the clock and we have police pickets on all roads. But it is not possible for us to be at every spot at all times. There cannot be foolproof arrangements. "Distribution of these vans is based on criteria like incidents of crime, population density, communal sensitivity and others. So the number of vans deployed in certain areas keeps changing according to crime graph and other factors."

Newsline looks at three lonely stretches at night.

RAJGHAT (Indraprastha Estate) to VIDHAN SABHA METRO

STATION (Chandrawal)

Distance: 6.8 km

Drive time: 12 min (approx)

The stretch has one picket at the left-hand turn from Rajghat to Metcalf House, usually unmanned, and another near Vidhan Sabha. Patrol vans are not stationed anywhere on the stretch and anyone in trouble near Metcalf House might find oneself stranded with mobile phone network missing.

UPPER RIDGE ROAD (Dhaula Kuan) to KAROL BAGH

Distance: 7.4 km

Drive time: 12 min (approx)

The road is flanked by the woods and is mostly deserted, with heavy vehicles plying. No PCR vans stationed in the area but some patrol the road at intervals.

ARUNA ASAF ALI MARG (JNU campus) to NELSON MANDELA MARG (Vasant Vihar)

Distance: 2.1 km

Drive time: 4 min (approx)

Deserted right from evening and has just one police picket. Mobile phone connectivity is lost near Inter University Accelerator Centre.

— Sweta Dutta

Heading: Gandhi smriti trailing mahatma’s steps - Indian Express
Content:
Students of St Angel's School, Rohini, attend the heritage walk at Gandhi Smriti conducted by The Indian Express and INTACH

A schools' initiative from The Express Group
Quest is a project conducted by The Indian Express in schools in and around Delhi. It covers more than 50 schools in Delhi and NCR.

Quest aims at stirring awareness and opinions. Today, when all that children see are shopping malls and cineplexes, we at The Indian Express want to show a completely different picture of this city to them. Delhi has changed beyond nostalgia and recognition since Independence. How many of these kids know of the 'Seven Cities' of Delhi or the stories of the pigeon fliers of Old Delhi?

The idea behind such an activity is to create awareness about the various structures and monuments that the students do not know about. This is a specially designed programme, which will help the students appreciate the rich culture and background of this city. In association with INTACH and ASI, this is a small effort on our behalf to depict a phase of our national life and the decay of a whole culture, a particular mode of thought and living. The visit is followed by the students sending in articles, pictures, poems, paintings, and collages to express their experiences about the heritage walk.

We invite schools to be a part of this

Express Group initiative.

TRIP TO "TEES JANUARY MARG" —A CURTAIN RAISER FOR YOUNG GENERATION
I was told that The Indian Express had organised a trip for our school to Gandhi Smriti. I was anxious to see the place where Gandhiji breathed his last. On the next day I was so excited that I could hardly wait till 8 am to get to school. I packed my bag with some snacks and water, and after a short journey of one and a half hours we reached Gandhi Smriti. It was very peaceful inside and there were lots of trees. We were then escorted by a volunteer who took us to the place where Nathuram Godse had fired three bullets at Gandhiji. We paid homage to the great man who led us to the path of non-violence. We also went to the room where he slept and the place where he met people. His stick, spoon and other belongings were displayed there and there was a big photograph of the last time he had chanted his prayers.

Inside the museum we saw a large gong and other musical instruments. In the hall we were shown an animation movie.

We saw a monitor which was movable: as it moved from right to left, it told us about Gandhiji, right from his birth till his struggles and his success in achieving freedom for India.

There was a room where the drawings made by children were hung on the walls. On the side of the walls, Gandhiji's famous "Three Monkeys" were drawn. On one side were traditional ones and on the other were modern forms of the monkeys.

There was a table on which stood the models of the people who followed Gandhiji's principles. They included Albert Einstein, Nelson Mandela, Dr S Radhakrishnan, Mohammad Ali Jinnah and many more.

The volunteer also told us that Gandhiji's last words were "Hey Ram".

This visit was full of knowledge and I learnt a lot about Gandhiji which I did not know earlier.

I would like to thank my teachers who selected me to go to the Smriti. It was once in a lifetime experience
- CHARU SHARMA X-C

A memory to cherish for life
All of us were quite excited when we got to know that we would be visiting Gandhi Smriti. Gandhiji, who was Bapu for everyone, can never be forgotten. His courage and inspiration were a motivation for one and all. He was a man of dignity, who followed the path of non-violence and peace.

I was enthusiastic about getting to see the place where he spent the last 144 days of his life. We first saw the death place of Gandhiji. "Hey Ram" were the last words spoken by him. We were also told by the guide why this place is known as Tees January Marg. When I saw Gandhiji's room, I had tears in my eyes. He lived in such simplicity.

We were also told the reason why he chose salt as a powerful weapon against British oppression — salt is a natural thing. Gandhiji said that no one should not be asked to pay tax for natural things like wind, air, water, fire, sky, as they all are available in nature. So he broke the salt law by manufacturing salt from sea water by boiling it.

As we entered the hall we were shown an animation movie which showcased how he was thrown out by the British from a train in South Africa.

Gandhiji used to pray everyday but on January 30, 1948, Gandhiji got late for the sabha, so he took a shortcut. Nathram Godse took advantage of this and fired three bullets in his body. I am very thankful to all my teachers and The Indian Express who gave me the opportunity of having such a scintillating experience.
- POOJA AGGARWAL, X-C

Housing The Mahatma's Message
Gandhi Smriti and Darshan Samiti (GSDS), an autonomous body, was formed in September 1984 by the merger of Gandhi Darshan at Rajghat and Gandhi Smriti, at 5, Tees January Marg. Gandhi Smriti, housed in Old Birla House on 5, Tees January Marg, is the place where the Mahatma was shot dead by Naturam Godse on January 30, 1948. The Mahatma had resided in Birla House from September 9, 1947. As a result, the house has memorabilia that defined the last 144 days of his life. The Old Birla House, acquired by the government in 1971, was converted into a national memorial for the Father of the Nation, and was opened to the public on August 15, 1973. The preserves include the room where Mahatma Gandhi lived and the prayer ground where he held a mass congregation every evening. The building and the landscape have been preserved as they were in the days of yore.

At the entrance of Gandhi Smriti is a life-like statue of the Mahatma standing on a globe, flanked by a boy and a girl. Sculpted by Shri Ram Sutar, the imagery symbolises Gandhi's empathy for the under-privileged and the downtrodden. The famous quotation — "My life is my message" — is inscribed on the statue. The museum's first floor houses the new-age Eternal Gandhi multimedia museum that presents his life through state-of-the-art, innovative installations, and technologically perceptive interfaces. There's the 'E-Prison', a timeline browser that tells the remarkable tale of Gandhiji's journey as a social revolutionary in search of spiritual enlightenment.

MAHATMA GANDHI
The man of honesty
The man of greatness
He is our Mahatma
The father of our nation!
Both in a family
Of cultured background
Grown is a circle.
Of loving parents
Honest, truthful and simple
Of body so frail yet nimble
With heart so big and true
With gifts but given to few.
Made many mistakes.
Realised his faults
Vowed never to commit them again.
Loved his motherland
Brought her freedom
With the weapon of Non - Violence
And not a drop of blood, shed.
Bravely to prison he went
Though so old and bent
Many a blow did he get
Yet never did he fret
With guns and knives, he did not fight
Satyagraha was his eternal might
India's Independence he fought and won
Bloodshed and bitterness there was none.
Adopted penance and fasting
Started the Satyagraha
Gave up foreign goods
And inspired wearing Khadi.
He is our only Gandhi
- ASHU PARASHER, X-A
